name: p4-0101-cpu-rings
title: CPU rings, privileged instructions, and fault handling
anchor: ### Why two modes? Kernel mode and user mode
spec: Concentric circle diagram illustrating x86 processor privilege levels and hardware fault isolation. Outer ring represents Ring 3 (User Mode / Unprivileged): contains user-space processes such as PyTorch, bash, web browser, and processes running as root (UID 0 in Ring 3). Unprivileged CPU instructions execute directly. Middle dividing boundary represents the CPU privilege barrier. Inner circle represents Ring 0 (Kernel Mode / Privileged): contains the Linux kernel, scheduler, virtual memory manager, device drivers (nvidia.ko, mlx5_core.ko), and kernel threads ([kthreadd], [kworker], [ksoftirqd]). Privileged CPU instructions (page table writes, direct device I/O, disabling interrupts) execute only here. Show two dynamic flows across the boundary: Flow 1 (Legitimate): User process invokes a system call (e.g., read(), open()), CPU performs controlled transition into Ring 0, kernel executes service and returns result to Ring 3. Flow 2 (Fault Trap): User process attempts a privileged CPU instruction directly; CPU hardware halts the instruction, raises a hardware fault/trap into Ring 0, and the kernel trap handler intercepts the fault and sends SIGSEGV/kills the rogue process while all other user processes and the kernel continue running unaffected. Include a side callout box contrasting failure scope: User process crash = local exit, kernel reclaims memory; Kernel bug/module fault = whole system halts with kernel panic.
alt: Concentric rings showing Ring 3 user mode and Ring 0 kernel mode, illustrating how CPU hardware traps illegal privileged instructions to protect the system.
cap: The CPU hardware boundary: user processes run in Ring 3 and trap into Ring 0 via system calls, while illegal privileged instructions trigger hardware faults that terminate the rogue process without halting the system.

name: p4-0101-device-files
title: Device file routing from user space to hardware and pseudodevices
spec: Three-tier architectural diagram illustrating how Linux routes standard file operations to devices. Top tier (User Space): Applications issue standard POSIX file system calls open(), read(), write(), and ioctl() on paths in /dev. Middle tier (Kernel Space): Divided into two pathways. Left pathway (Hardware-backed device nodes): Special character device /dev/nvidia0 and block device /dev/nvme0n1. The VFS and device subsystem map open() and ioctl() requests to loaded kernel modules (nvidia.ko and nvme.ko). Modules reside in kernel space as .ko objects. Right pathway (Pseudodevices): Software-only devices in /dev that correspond to no hardware. /dev/null routes writes to a kernel sink that discards bytes; /dev/zero routes reads to a kernel generator returning 0x00 bytes; /dev/urandom routes reads to the kernel cryptographic entropy pool. Bottom tier (Physical Hardware vs Pure Software): Left pathway connects drivers to physical PCIe hardware (NVIDIA H100 GPU and NVMe SSD). Right pathway connects pseudodevices to pure in-kernel software routines with no physical hardware backing.
alt: Diagram illustrating how file operations on device nodes under slash dev route through kernel device drivers to physical hardware or software pseudodevices.
cap: Linux device architecture: ordinary file system calls on files under slash dev are routed by the kernel to either hardware device drivers or kernel-internal pseudodevices.

name: p4-0101-syscall-boundary
title: The system call execution path and category routing
anchor: ### Job 4: system calls and the services around them
spec: Sequence and flow diagram detailing how a request traverses from an application into kernel subsystems. Top layer (User Space Application): User program executes code and calls a high-level C library function such as open('data.txt'), malloc(), socket(), or clone(). Second layer (User Space Library): glibc (libc.so.6) receives the call, places arguments into CPU architecture registers, sets the system call opcode number (e.g., __NR_openat), and executes the hardware syscall instruction. Boundary: Horizontal dashed line representing the User/Kernel boundary (CPU switches from Ring 3 to Ring 0). An strace callout box points to this exact line, showing that strace intercepts every crossing via ptrace and records call name, arguments, and return codes. Third layer (Kernel Space System Call Dispatcher): Syscall handler reads opcode and branches into five distinct kernel functional categories: 1. Files (openat, read, write, close, stat); 2. Processes (clone, execve, wait4, exit_group, kill); 3. Memory (mmap, brk, munmap, mprotect); 4. Network (socket, connect, bind, listen, accept, sendto, recvfrom); 5. Control and Info (ioctl, getpid, uname, clock_gettime). Bottom return arrow: The subsystem returns status/value to dispatcher, CPU switches back to Ring 3, and glibc sets errno or returns result to user application.
alt: Diagram of a system call journey showing user code calling glibc, transitioning through the CPU syscall instruction into kernel subsystems, with strace intercepting at the boundary.
cap: The system call path: user applications invoke glibc wrappers that trigger the hardware syscall instruction, transitioning execution to the kernel dispatcher across five functional categories while strace observes the boundary.

name: p4-0101-rhel-lineage
title: The Red Hat upstream-to-downstream distribution river
anchor: ### 6.1 The Red Hat, Fedora, CentOS, and Amazon Linux branch
spec: Vertical river-flow diagram illustrating the Red Hat enterprise distribution lineage from upstream development to downstream production. Top tier (Upstream): Fedora Project. Sponsored by Red Hat; fast release cycle (every 6 months); incorporates cutting-edge upstream Linux kernels, gcc, systemd, and glibc; acts as community testbed. Middle tier (Midstream): CentOS Stream. Acts as a rolling-preview midstream between Fedora and RHEL; incorporates stabilized upstream packages before commercial freeze. Main branch (Downstream Commercial): Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL). Long-term commercial stability, vendor hardware/ISV certifications (Slurm, NVIDIA drivers, Base Command Manager), backported kernel features (e.g., 5.14 kernel backports in RHEL 9). Downstream community and cloud derivatives branching from RHEL source code: 1. Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux: 1:1 bug-for-bug binary compatible free rebuilds created after CentOS moved to Stream; 2. Amazon Linux 2023 (AL2023): AWS cloud-tailored distribution incorporating Fedora, CentOS Stream, and RHEL source components; 3. Oracle Linux: alternative enterprise rebuild. Surrounding toolchain bracket: Highlights shared package ecosystem across all members: RPM package format (.rpm), low-level tool rpm, and high-level repository resolvers yum and modern dnf.
alt: Lineage diagram showing the flow of packages from upstream Fedora through midstream CentOS Stream to downstream RHEL and binary rebuilds Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, and Amazon Linux.
cap: The Red Hat distribution lineage: innovations flow from upstream Fedora through midstream CentOS Stream to RHEL, which downstream community distributions like Rocky Linux and cloud distributions like Amazon Linux rebuild or adapt using RPM and DNF.

name: p4-0102-builtin-cwd
title: Why cd and export must be builtins: process boundaries and working directory isolation
anchor: ### The forms of the basic commands
spec: Two-panel comparison diagram illustrating process boundaries during command execution. Left panel ('Hypothetical External /bin/cd /tmp'): Shows Process 1 'Interactive Shell' (PID 1000, CWD: /home/alice). Shell calls fork() and execve() to spawn Process 2 'Child /bin/cd' (PID 1001, inherits CWD: /home/alice). Child process executes chdir('/tmp'), updating its own CWD to /tmp. Child process terminates (exit 0). Arrow points back to Process 1: Parent Shell CWD remains unchanged at /home/alice because the kernel strictly isolates process memory and task structures. Callout: 'Directory change is lost upon child exit'. Right panel ('Actual Shell Builtin: cd /tmp'): Shows Process 1 'Interactive Shell' (PID 1000, CWD: /home/alice). Shell parses command 'cd' and identifies it as an internal builtin. No fork() occurs. Parent Shell directly invokes the kernel system call chdir('/tmp') within its own process context. Shell CWD updates to /tmp. Bottom summary bar lists other state-modifying builtins that cannot run as child processes: export (environment block), alias (shell lookup table), umask (file creation mask), and source / . (executing script in current shell).
alt: A comparison showing why an external cd command changes only its own child process directory before exiting, whereas a shell builtin changes the working directory of the interactive shell itself.
cap: A child process cannot alter its parent process environment or working directory, so commands like cd and export must execute directly inside the shell as builtins.

name: p4-0102-readline-map
title: Readline keyboard shortcuts and line-editing buffer motions

Bottom section illustrates text deletion and the kill ring: backward span over '--batch-size ' labeled 'Ctrl-W (erase word)'; broad left span from cursor to start of line labeled 'Ctrl-U (erase to start)'; broad right span from cursor to end of line labeled 'Ctrl-K (erase to end)'. name: p4-0103-paths-traversal
title: Absolute versus Relative Path Resolution from Working Directory
anchor: ## 1. Paths: how you name a file
spec: Tree topology diagram illustrating path navigation. At top: Root directory '/' box. Branch left: '/home' -> '/home/alice' -> '/home/alice/project' -> file 'train.py'. Callout label: 'Absolute Path: /home/alice/project/train.py (starts with /, identical target from any process)'. Branch right: '/usr' with subdirectories '/usr/lib' and '/usr/bin'. Current Working Directory (pwd) indicator highlighted around '/usr/lib'. Relative path navigation arrows radiating from '/usr/lib': (1) self-reference '.' staying at '/usr/lib'; (2) downward traversal './X11' or 'X11' reaching '/usr/lib/X11'; (3) upward traversal '..' moving up to parent '/usr'; (4) composite traversal '../bin' moving up to '..' (/usr) then down to 'bin' (/usr/bin). Bottom callout box: '~ shorthand expands in shell to user home directory (e.g. /home/alice), never seen directly by kernel.'
alt: Diagram illustrating absolute path resolution starting at root slash and relative path navigation from current working directory usr lib using dot and dot-dot.
cap: Absolute paths always resolve from root slash, while relative paths depend on the process current working directory with dot representing current and dot-dot representing parent directory.

name: p4-0103-hard-vs-symlink
title: Structural Comparison of Hard Links versus Symbolic Links
spec: Two-panel comparative architecture diagram. Left panel (Hard Links): Directory table contains two separate name entries 'a.txt' and 'b.txt'. Both entries point directly to the same Inode record 'Inode 7401'. Inode 7401 box displays: 'Type: regular (-)', 'Link count: 2', 'Size: 200 MiB', and data block pointers targeting data block containing payload bytes 'hello'. Annotation: 'rm a.txt' deletes directory entry 'a.txt' and decrements link count to 1; data blocks remain intact and accessible via 'b.txt'. Boundary note: 'EXDEV error: Hard links cannot cross mount points/filesystems (e.g. ext4 to tmpfs)'. Right panel (Symbolic Links): Directory table contains entry 'cuda' pointing to 'Inode 5520'. Inode 5520 box displays: 'Type: symbolic link (l)', 'Link count: 1', 'Size: 21 bytes'. Its data block stores target string path '/usr/local/cuda-12.4'. A resolution arrow points from that path string to the target directory 'cuda-12.4' (Inode 3105). Annotation: If 'cuda-12.4' is moved or deleted, 'cuda' becomes a dangling link pointing to nowhere. Capability note: 'Symlinks can cross filesystem boundaries and point to directories.'
alt: Side by side comparison showing a hard link sharing an inode record and a symbolic link containing a target path string with dangling behavior on deletion.
cap: Hard links create multiple directory entries for a single inode that survive deletion of other names, whereas symbolic links store path strings that become dangling if the target is moved or deleted.

name: p4-0103-atomic-symlink-swap
title: Two-Step Atomic Symlink Replacement Workflow
spec: Three-stage workflow sequence diagram showing safe checkpoint pointer rotation. Initial State (T0): Directory contains checkpoint directories 'checkpoints/step_000900' and 'checkpoints/step_001000'. Active symlink 'latest' points to 'step_000900'. Concurrent Reader process resolves 'latest/model.pt' -> 'step_000900/model.pt'. Step 1 (T1 - Prepare): Command 'ln -sfn checkpoints/step_001000 latest.tmp'. A temporary symlink 'latest.tmp' is created pointing to 'step_001000'. The existing 'latest' symlink remains untouched and live. Concurrent Readers during T1 still resolve 'step_000900' with zero errors. Step 2 (T2 - Atomic Swap): Command 'mv -T latest.tmp latest'. The Linux kernel executes an atomic rename() syscall, replacing 'latest' with 'latest.tmp' in a single filesystem operation. Final State: 'latest' now points to 'step_001000'. 'latest.tmp' disappears. Callout highlight: Readers at all moments see either step_000900 or step_001000, never encountering a missing link window (ENOENT).
alt: Two-step sequence diagram illustrating creation of latest.tmp pointing to new checkpoint step followed by atomic rename over latest to prevent reader race conditions.
cap: Creating latest.tmp before executing an atomic rename over latest ensures continuous resolution for reader processes with zero downtime window.

name: p4-0103-tar-compression-pipeline
title: Tar Archiving Pipeline and Compressor Trade-off Comparison
spec: Top: Two-stage archiving and compression pipeline. Stage 1 (Archive): Multiple directory tree files ('project/code.py', 'project/config.yaml', 'project/model.safetensors') with individual metadata (permissions, owner, mtime) enter 'tar -c', bundling into a continuous sequential tar stream. Stage 2 (Compress): Tar stream passes through compressor tool ('gzip', 'bzip2', 'xz', 'zstd') creating single archive file (e.g. 'project.tar.gz' via 'tar -czf' or 'project.tar.zst' via 'tar --zstd -f'). Reverse flow indicates 'tar -tf' lists and verifies table of contents, while 'tar -xzf -C /target' extracts into dedicated folder. Bottom: Comparative trade-off matrix across 4 compressors: (1) gzip (-z): fast compression, moderate ratio, single/multi-core via pigz, ubiquitous standard for logs/configs; (2) bzip2 (-j): slower compression, higher ratio, pbzip2, legacy text; (3) xz (-J): very slow compression, maximum ratio, xz -T0, software release tarballs; (4) zstd (--zstd): very fast gzip-like speed, high compression ratio, zstd -T0, modern AI default for checkpoints/datasets. Callout rule: 'Do not compress already compressed files (.safetensors, .pt, .zip); wastes CPU with zero byte reduction.'
alt: Flow diagram of two-stage tar archiving and compression pipeline with a comparison matrix of gzip, bzip2, xz, and zstd compressors.
cap: Archiving bundles files and metadata into a stream while compression shrinks the bytes, with zstd and pigz providing modern speed and ratio trade-offs for AI workloads.

name: p4-0104-cut-vs-awk-delim
title: Field Splitting: Single Delimiter in cut Versus Whitespace Collapsing in awk
spec: Top: A single text line from a ps table: 'root      1024  0.0  0.1 slurmd', where 'root' and '1024' are separated by six space characters. Middle path labeled 'cut -d" "': each individual space character forms a delimiter boundary. Field 1 contains 'root'. Delimiter 1 creates empty Field 2 (''). Delimiter 2 creates empty Field 3 (''). Delimiters 3 through 5 create empty Fields 4, 5, and 6 (''). Delimiter 6 leaves '1024' in Field 7. A red crossout callout highlights 'cut -d" " -f2 returns empty string (fails to extract PID)'. Bottom path labeled 'awk default splitting': contiguous whitespace runs are collapsed into a single delimiter, and leading whitespace is stripped. Box $1 contains 'root'. Six collapsed spaces lead directly to Box $2 containing '1024'. Two collapsed spaces lead to Box $3 containing '0.0'. Two collapsed spaces lead to Box $4 containing '0.1'. One space leads to Box $5 containing 'slurmd'. A green checkmark callout shows 'awk "{print \$2, \$5}" returns 1024 slurmd'.
alt: Comparison of how cut and awk split a space-aligned table line into fields.
cap: cut treats every individual space as a delimiter and produces empty fields on aligned tables, while awk collapses runs of whitespace.

name: p4-0104-comm-columns
title: Three-Column Comparison and Suppression Flags in comm
spec: Left: Two sorted input files. File A contains lines ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']. File B contains lines ['banana', 'cherry', 'date']. Center: Standard output of 'comm fileA fileB' showing three tab-delimited columns. Column 1 (no leading tab) displays lines unique to File A: 'apple'. Column 2 (one leading tab) displays lines unique to File B: 'date'. Column 3 (two leading tabs) displays lines common to both files: 'banana' and 'cherry'. Right: A decision table mapping suppression flags to set operations. 'comm -12 fileA fileB' shows -1 hiding Column 1 and -2 hiding Column 2, leaving only Column 3 (Intersection: lines in both). 'comm -23 fileA fileB' shows -2 and -3 hiding Columns 2 and 3, leaving only Column 1 (Set difference: File A minus File B). 'comm -13 fileA fileB' shows -1 and -3 hiding Columns 1 and 3, leaving only Column 2 (Set difference: File B minus File A). An annotation note emphasizes: 'comm flags suppress columns rather than select them, and inputs must be sorted beforehand.'
alt: Diagram showing comm three-column output format and column suppression flags.
cap: comm outputs three columns for lines unique to file A, unique to file B, and common to both, where flags suppress rather than select columns.

name: p4-0105-ssh-keypairs
title: Host Key versus User Key: Trust Direction and File Locations
spec: Two-lane architecture diagram comparing the two distinct key pairs in an SSH session. Top lane (Server Authentication / Host Key): Left box 'Client (Laptop)' containing '~/.ssh/known_hosts' (mode 0644). Right box 'Server (gpu01)' containing '/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key' (private, mode 0600) and 'ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub' (public, mode 0644). Arrow from Server to Client: 'Server proves identity with Host Key signature on key exchange' -> Client verifies against 'known_hosts' fingerprint. Protects against Man-in-the-Middle attacks. Bottom lane (User Authentication / User Key): Left box 'Client (Laptop)' containing '~/.ssh/id_ed25519' (private key, mode 0600, passphrase protected) and '~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub' (public key, mode 0644). Right box 'Server (gpu01)' containing target user's '~/.ssh/authorized_keys' (mode 0600) inside '~/.ssh' (mode 0700) within '~/' (mode 0750/0755, non-writable by group/others). Arrow from Client to Server: 'Client proves identity by signing server challenge with user private key' -> Server verifies signature against public key in 'authorized_keys'. Highlights StrictModes permission callout box on both sides.
alt: Comparison of server host key and client user key storage, file permissions, and cryptographic trust directions.
cap: Two key pairs secure an SSH session: the host key authenticates the server to the client, while the user key authenticates the client to the server.

name: p4-0105-tmux-architecture
title: Process Lifecycle Under tmux: Isolating Processes from SIGHUP
spec: Split-panel comparison of process lifecycles during network disconnection. Panel A (Without tmux: Plain SSH): Box 'Client' running 'ssh user@gpu01' over TCP to Box 'Remote Server'. On remote server, process tree shows 'sshd (daemon)' -> child 'sshd (privsep session)' allocating pseudo-terminal '/dev/pts/1' -> 'bash (login shell)' -> foreground process 'python train.py'. Red lightning bolt 'Network Drop / Laptop Sleep' breaks TCP connection. Consequence: 'sshd session' terminates, '/dev/pts/1' hangs up, kernel sends 'SIGHUP' to foreground process group -> 'python train.py' killed. Panel B (With tmux: Persistent Multiplexer): Box 'Client' running 'ssh -t gpu01 tmux attach' over TCP. On remote server, 'sshd session' runs transient 'tmux client' talking over local Unix socket '/tmp/tmux-UID/default' to background 'tmux server (daemon)'. The persistent 'tmux server' owns virtual ptys: '/dev/pts/2' running 'bash' and 'python train.py'. Red lightning bolt 'Network Drop' or user 'Ctrl-b d (detach)' terminates only transient 'sshd' and 'tmux client'. Consequence: 'tmux server' and 'python train.py' continue running unharmed. Green reconnect arrow shows subsequent 'tmux attach -t train' re-establishing visual output.
alt: Architecture diagram showing how tmux isolates running processes from SIGHUP when an SSH connection drops.
cap: tmux decouples processes from the interactive terminal, allowing jobs to persist on the server even when the SSH client disconnects.

name: p4-0105-vim-modes
title: Vim Modal Editing State Machine and Key Transitions
spec: State machine diagram showing Vim modes and keystroke transitions. Central node (Initial State): 'Normal Mode' (Navigation & Command Execution: 'x' delete char, 'dd' cut line, 'yy' yank line, 'p' paste, 'u' undo, 'Ctrl-r' redo, '/word' search, 'gg'/'G' top/bottom). Transition 1 to top-right node 'Insert Mode' (Text entry): forward arrow labeled 'i' (insert at cursor) or 'a' (append); return arrow labeled 'Esc' returning to Normal Mode. Transition 2 to bottom-right node 'Visual Mode' (Text selection): forward arrow labeled 'v' (character visual) or 'V' (line visual); return arrow labeled 'Esc' returning to Normal Mode. Box notes operations like 'd' (delete) or 'y' (yank) apply to highlighted selection and return to Normal Mode. Transition 3 to bottom-left node 'Command-Line Mode' (Ex commands): forward arrow labeled ':' from Normal Mode. Shows screen-bottom prompt ':' with key commands listed: ':w' (save buffer), ':q' (quit), ':wq' (save & quit), ':q!' (force quit discarding changes), ':%s/old/new/g' (global substitution). Return arrow labeled 'Enter' (executes) or 'Esc' (cancels) returning to Normal Mode. Callout box on safe editing: 'cp -a config config.bak' -> 'sudoedit config' -> 'diff -u' -> syntax check ('sshd -t') -> reload.
alt: State machine diagram showing transitions between Vim normal, insert, visual, and command-line modes.
cap: Vim operates as a modal state machine where key presses trigger commands in normal mode, text entry in insert mode, selections in visual mode, and file actions in command-line mode.

name: p4-0105-timeout-refused
title: Diagnostic Decision Tree: SSH Timeout versus Connection Refused
spec: Three-way diagnostic branching flowchart starting from command 'ssh user@host -p 22'. Branch 1 (Hangs 30-120 s, then 'Connection timed out' / ETIMEDOUT): Packet path shows Client sending TCP SYN -> packet dropped silently by Firewall, Cloud Security Group (GCP/AWS), routing black hole, or host is powered off. No packet returns. Action step: 'ping host', 'traceroute -T -p 22 host', check cloud VPC security group egress/ingress rules, verify host power via BMC. Branch 2 (Fails immediately in 0.01 s, 'Connection refused' / ECONNREFUSED): Packet path shows Client sending TCP SYN -> reaches server IP and network stack successfully -> Server kernel finds no process listening on TCP port 22 -> Server kernel immediately returns TCP RST/ACK. Action step: 'nc -vz host 22', on server check 'systemctl status sshd' and 'ss -tlnp | grep :22' (sshd dead or bound to non-default port). Branch 3 (TCP handshake succeeds SYN/ACK, but hangs before login): Packet path shows TCP connection established, but stalls during SSH version string exchange ('SSH-2.0-...'). Action step: 'ssh -vvv host' to check MTU fragmentation or hung sshd process.
alt: Diagnostic flowchart contrasting the causes and network signatures of an SSH connection timeout versus connection refused.
cap: An SSH timeout indicates silent packet drops along the network path, whereas connection refused confirms the host responded with a TCP reset because no service was listening on port 22.

name: p4-0106-dir-traversal
title: Directory Traversal Versus File Access and Deletion Permissions
anchor: ### What the bits mean: files versus directories
spec: A three-panel diagram demonstrating the kernel's distinct permission evaluation for directories versus files. Panel A (Path Traversal for 'cat /data/project/file'): Show a horizontal path hierarchy '[ / ] (root)' -> '[ /data ]' -> '[ /data/project ]' -> '[ file ]'. Label the directory check on each: requires 'x' (traverse inode). Step 1 checks '/' (needs x, granted). Step 2 checks '/data' (needs x, granted). Step 3 checks '/data/project' (needs x). Show two outcomes: if 'x' is granted, the kernel proceeds to 'file' and evaluates 'r' (read content); if 'x' is missing on '/data/project' (even if 'r' is set or file mode is 0777), the kernel immediately aborts with 'EACCES: Permission denied'. Panel B (File Deletion Mechanism for 'rm /data/project/file'): Box representing directory inode '/data/project' containing directory table entries '[ inode 4821 | file ]'. Inside it sits 'file' with mode '0444 (r--r--r--)'. Show an actor 'Bob' executing 'rm /data/project/file'. Draw an arrow showing the kernel checking write ('w') and execute ('x') exclusively on the parent directory inode '/data/project'. An unlinking action crosses out the entry in the directory table. Emphasize with a callout that deletion mutates the directory table, not the file contents, allowing Bob to delete a read-only 0444 file without write permission on the file itself. Panel C (Sticky Bit Defense on '/tmp' mode 1777 / 'drwxrwxrwt'): Show directory '/tmp' with sticky bit ('t'). Bob attempts 'rm /tmp/alice_temp.txt'. Show the kernel check: Bob is neither file owner (alice) nor directory owner (root) nor root, so the delete fails with 'EPERM: Operation not permitted'.
alt: A diagram showing how directory path traversal requires execute permissions on every parent directory while file deletion depends on write permission in the parent directory.
cap: Path traversal checks execute permission at every path segment, and file deletion modifies the directory inode rather than the file itself.

name: p4-0106-shared-dir-recipe
title: Safe Shared Directory Mechanics: setgid Group Inheritance and umask Coordination
anchor: ### A recipe: a safe shared project directory
spec: A side-by-side workflow diagram contrasting the default Linux file creation failure against the safe shared project directory pattern. Left Column (Default Failure): Directory '/data/projx' has mode '0755' (drwxr-xr-x), owned by 'root:projx'. Alice (primary group 'alice', supplementary group 'projx', umask '022') creates 'notes.txt'. The kernel assigns owner 'alice:1042', group 'alice:1042' (inheriting creator primary group), and mode '0644 (rw-r--r--)'. Bob (supplementary group 'projx') attempts write access ('echo data >> notes.txt'). The kernel evaluates Bob under 'Other (r--)' because group does not match; write is denied ('Permission denied'). Right Column (The 2770 Recipe): Directory '/data/projx' is configured with 'chmod 2770' (drwxrws---) and group 'projx:2001', highlighting the 's' in the group execute position (setgid bit 2000). Alice sets 'umask 002' in her startup environment. Alice runs 'touch notes.txt'. Show two arrows: Arrow 1 from parent directory enforces group inheritance via setgid, setting file group to 'projx:2001'. Arrow 2 from umask 002 retains group write permission, setting file mode to '0664 (rw-rw-r--)'. Bob (member of 'projx') writes to 'notes.txt'. The kernel matches Bob's supplementary group 'projx' to the file group; write is granted ('rw-'). Outside users ('Other: ---') have zero access.
alt: A comparison of default file creation resulting in permission denial versus a setgid 2770 directory with umask 002 enabling shared group collaboration.
cap: The setgid bit on a directory forces new files to inherit the parent group while umask 002 preserves group write permissions for teammates.

name: p4-0106-ldap-storm-sssd
title: Standalone LDAP Connection Storm Versus Node-Local SSSD Caching at Scale
anchor: ### 8.4 LDAP, explosive job-launch storms, and SSSD caching
spec: A two-part architectural failure cascade and resolution diagram. Top Panel (The Job-Launch Storm on Standalone LDAP): Slurm workload manager initiates a 500-node training job at time t=0 across nodes 'gpu001' to 'gpu500'. Each node's process executes 'getpwnam(alice)'. 500 concurrent TCP and TLS connection arrows converge simultaneously on a single central box: 'Central Standalone LDAP Server (port 636)'. Inside the LDAP server, show a queue container with 'Worker Thread Pool: 64 threads (saturated)'. Excess connection arrows overflow the TCP backlog queue, resulting in connection timeouts and dropped packets. Compute nodes whose queries time out return an error; Slurm step launch fails across affected nodes with 'slurmstepd: error: user alice not found'. Bottom Panel (Mitigation via Node-Local SSSD Caching): The same 500 compute nodes receive the Slurm launch trigger. On each compute node, the process calls 'getpwnam(alice)'. The C library NSS module delegates over a local Unix domain socket '/var/run/sssd/sssd.pipe' to a node-local 'SSSD Daemon'. SSSD performs an in-memory/LDB database lookup on '/var/lib/sss/db/cache_cluster.ldb'. The lookup succeeds locally in under 1 millisecond with zero network round trips, allowing all 500 nodes to launch the job steps immediately. A single dashed background arrow connects SSSD to the Central LDAP Server for periodic asynchronous background cache updates, eliminating query storms.
alt: A diagram comparing a 500-node LDAP connection storm that drops requests against node-local SSSD caching that resolves queries locally in under one millisecond.
cap: A standalone LDAP server drops requests during synchronized multi-node job launches unless node-local SSSD caches absorb the query burst.

name: p4-0108-lsof-cols
title: Anatomy of lsof Command Output
spec: Command-output anatomy diagram breaking down the 9 columns of lsof based on the chapter listing: COMMAND, PID, USER, FD, TYPE, DEVICE, SIZE/OFF, NODE, NAME. Show sample rows from text: (1) 'systemd 1 root cwd DIR 8,1 4096 2 /', (2) 'systemd 1 root txt REG 8,1 1595792 9961784 /lib/systemd/systemd', and (3) 'vi 1994 juser 3u REG 8,1 12288 786440 /tmp/.ff.swp'. Use callout brackets with descriptive annotations for key columns: FD column callout highlights role strings ('cwd' = current working directory, 'txt' = executable text, 'mem' = mapped library) versus numeric open file descriptors with access mode ('3u' = descriptor 3 opened for read-write); TYPE callout highlights 'DIR' (directory) and 'REG' (regular file); DEVICE callout points to major,minor disk device numbers ('8,1'); NODE callout points to filesystem inode number ('786440'); NAME callout points to filesystem path or target.
alt: Anatomy of lsof columns mapping process credentials, file descriptor types and numbers, and filesystem nodes.
cap: The lsof command exposes process ownership, descriptor roles like cwd or descriptor 3u, filesystem node IDs, and device numbers.

name: p4-0108-priority-classes
title: Linux Task Priority Controls: Nice, Ionice, and CPU Affinity
spec: Three-panel architectural diagram illustrating the three dimensions of Linux task priority discussed in Section 6. Left panel: 'CPU Niceness' showing the scale from -20 (highest priority, least nice, root only) through 0 (default) to +19 (lowest priority, most nice). Show kernel dynamic priority PR = 20 + NI and sample commands: 'nice -n 15 ./long_job.sh' and 'renice -n 10 -p 3322'. Center panel: 'Block I/O Priority (ionice)' showing the 3 classes: Class 1 Real-time (-c 1, served first, root only); Class 2 Best-effort (-c 2, levels 0 to 7, default 4); Class 3 Idle (-c 3, served only when disk has no other traffic). Show sample command: 'ionice -c 3 nice -n 19 rsync -a src/ dst/'. Right panel: 'CPU and NUMA Affinity' showing taskset core pinning (e.g. cores 0-7 via 'taskset -c 0-7 ./prog') and NUMA memory and CPU binding via 'numactl --cpunodebind=1 --membind=1 python train.py'.
alt: Three dimensions of Linux task priority: CPU niceness from -20 to 19, disk IO classes 1 through 3, and CPU core affinity.
cap: Combining nice, ionice, and taskset or numactl controls CPU shares, disk scheduling priority, and NUMA core pinning independently.

name: p4-0109-getopts-trace
title: Trace of getopts Parsing Flags, Advancing OPTIND, and Shifting Positional Arguments
spec: A step-by-step trace diagram illustrating how while getopts ":hn:t:" opt processes command-line arguments and updates internal pointers. Top section: Input argument array with 6 boxes representing positional parameters: [1: "-n"], [2: "4"], [3: "-t"], [4: "/data"], [5: "train.py"], [6: "run42"]. Middle section shows 3 sequential iterations: Step 1 (Parsing -n): getopts inspects index 1 ("-n"); matches 'n:' which expects an argument; consumes index 2 ("4"); variable opt is assigned "n"; variable OPTARG is assigned "4"; internal pointer OPTIND advances from 1 to 3 (pointing to index 3). Step 2 (Parsing -t): getopts inspects index 3 ("-t"); matches 't:' which expects an argument; consumes index 4 ("/data"); opt is assigned "t"; OPTARG is assigned "/data"; internal pointer OPTIND advances from 3 to 5 (pointing to index 5). Step 3 (Non-option terminator): getopts inspects index 5 ("train.py"); encounters no leading hyphen; getopts returns exit code 1; while loop terminates; OPTIND remains 5. Bottom section (The shift operation): Shows command shift $((OPTIND - 1)) evaluated as shift 4; a scissor or slice icon removes arguments 1 through 4 ("-n", "4", "-t", "/data"); shows remaining positional arguments array where $1 becomes "train.py" and $2 becomes "run42", ready to be consumed via "$@".
alt: Step-by-step trace of getopts parsing short options and arguments, advancing OPTIND from 1 to 5, and shifting off processed flags.
cap: How getopts iterates over flags and values, updates OPTIND, and hands remaining arguments to the script via shift.

name: p4-0111-syscall-mechanism
title: System Call Execution Path, Errno Handling, and vDSO Bypass
spec: Split diagram into two horizontal privilege domains separated by a thick dashed hardware boundary line: User Space (Ring 3) on top, and Kernel Space (Ring 0) below. On the left side, show the standard system call flow (e.g. openat): 1. User Application issues open('data.bin', O_RDONLY). 2. C Library Wrapper (libc) places syscall number into register rax (e.g. 257 for sys_openat) and argument pointers into rdi, rsi, rdx. 3. Wrapper executes the syscall instruction (or svc on ARM64). 4. Downward arrow crossing into Kernel Space (Ring 0): CPU switches to kernel mode at fixed entry point. 5. Kernel inspects system call table (sys_call_table[rax]) to dispatch sys_openat(). 6. Kernel performs filesystem traversal and permission checks; if path does not exist, kernel returns negative error number -ENOENT (-2) in rax. 7. Upward arrow crossing boundary back to User Space: CPU switches back to Ring 3. 8. C Wrapper inspects rax, detects negative value, copies positive 2 into thread-local variable errno (ENOENT), and returns -1 to Application. Application calls perror() or strerror(errno) to print 'No such file or directory'. On the right side, show the vDSO bypass path: User Application calls clock_gettime() or gettimeofday(). An arrow bypasses the Ring 0 boundary entirely, redirecting directly into the [vdso] memory page mapped by the kernel into process user space. Reading occurs entirely in Ring 3 with no context switch and no mode switch, annotated with callout: 'Invisible to strace and ptrace'.
alt: A diagram contrasting the full kernel-switch system call path with register handling and errno translation against the user-space vDSO bypass.
cap: A system call transitions from user space to kernel space via CPU registers and the syscall instruction, with libc mapping negative returns to errno; vDSO calls execute entirely in user space.

name: p4-0111-futex-and-false-sharing
title: Hybrid Futex Lock Escalation and Cache Line False Sharing
spec: Two side-by-side technical diagrams. Left panel: 'Hybrid Futex Escalation (pthread_mutex)'. Show a vertical 3-tier flowchart: Tier 1 at top: 'Atomic Compare-and-Swap (CAS) in User Space'. Uncontended lock acquired immediately via single CPU atomic instruction (~10-20 ns, zero syscall overhead). If locked, arrow points down to Tier 2: 'Adaptive Spin Loop'. Waiter thread spins briefly in user space checking lock variable if the lock owner is active on another CPU core. If released during spin, lock acquired. If still locked, arrow points down to Tier 3: 'futex(addr, FUTEX_WAIT_PRIVATE, val) Syscall'. Waiter traps into kernel, context-switches off CPU, and sleeps on kernel futex wait queue. Once owner releases, it calls futex(addr, FUTEX_WAKE, 1) to wake waiter. Annotation notes: 'futex syscall only appears in strace during heavy lock contention'. Right panel: 'False Sharing on 64-Byte Cache Line'. Draw two CPU Cores (Core 0 and Core 1). Between them, draw a single 64-byte L1 cache line containing two independent variables: var_a (modified by Thread 0 on Core 0) and var_b (modified by Thread 1 on Core 1). Show alternating red flash arrows: Core 0 writes var_a, forcing CPU interconnect cache invalidation (MESI protocol) of Core 1's cache line; Core 1 writes var_b, invalidating Core 0's cache line. Annotated penalty: 'Severe interconnect bus traffic and latency degradation despite independent code'. Below it, show the fix: alignas(64) padding pushing var_a and var_b into separate 64-byte cache lines.
alt: Diagram showing the 3-tier hybrid futex escalation from user-space atomic CAS to sleeping syscall, alongside false sharing on a 64-byte CPU cache line.
cap: Hybrid futex locks escalate from user-space atomic operations to kernel sleeps only under contention, while false sharing degrades multi-threaded performance across shared 64-byte cache lines.

name: p4-0111-frame-pointer-unwind
title: Call Stack Unwinding via Frame Pointers versus Truncated Stacks
anchor: ### Gotchas: missing symbols and missing stacks
spec: Two comparative vertical columns showing stack memory layout during CPU profiling with perf record -g. Left column: 'Intact Frame Pointer Chain (-fno-omit-frame-pointer)'. Show three stacked stack frames in memory: Frame 0 (main), Frame 1 (work), Frame 2 (sqrt). Inside each frame, show local variables, Saved RIP (return instruction pointer), and Saved RBP (base/frame pointer). Green arrows link the RBP chain: CPU register RBP points to Frame 2's Saved RBP, which points directly up to Frame 1's Saved RBP, which points up to Frame 0's Saved RBP. A profiler side-bracket shows perf reading each Saved RIP at fixed offsets from RBP, walking the full chain to generate a complete 3-level flame graph stack (main -> work -> sqrt). Right column: 'Broken Stack (-fomit-frame-pointer)'. Show the same three frames, but with RBP omitted from stack frames and repurposed by compiler as a general-purpose register holding an arbitrary runtime calculation value (e.g. counter integer 42). Profiler reads RBP, treats 42 as a memory address, triggers invalid dereference or immediate unwinder halt at Frame 2. Result callout below: flame graph displays only a truncated 1-level stack or [unknown] hex address, hiding the caller hierarchy. Callout boxes list remedies: -fno-omit-frame-pointer, JVM -XX:+PreserveFramePointer, or perf --call-graph dwarf.
alt: Diagram comparing intact call stack unwinding via RBP frame pointers against a truncated call stack caused by -fomit-frame-pointer.
cap: Frame pointers maintain a linked chain of Saved RBP addresses on the stack that profilers walk; omitting frame pointers repurposes RBP, truncating profiles into single frames or unknown addresses.

name: p4-0112-512e-rmw
title: The 512e Read-Modify-Write Penalty
spec: A comparative architectural diagram in two panels (A and B) contrasting an aligned write with an unaligned 512-byte write on a 512e Advanced Format drive. Panel A (Aligned 4 KiB Write): Top box shows 'Application Buffer: 4,096 Bytes (Aligned to 4 KiB offset 0)'. A straight green arrow labelled 'Single Direct Write (1 I/O operation)' points down to 'Drive Controller RAM Buffer' and then directly to 'Physical NAND / Platter: Physical Sector 0 (4,096 Bytes)'. Metrics box below shows: 'Read count: 0, Write count: 1, Total operations: 1'. Panel B (Unaligned 512-Byte Write - Read-Modify-Write): Top box shows 'Application Buffer: 512 Bytes (Targeting logical sector 1, offset 512-1023)'. Three sequential numbered steps: Step 1 (Read): A blue arrow labelled '1. Read entire 4 KiB physical sector' pulls Physical Sector 0 (4,096 bytes) from physical disk into 'Drive Controller DRAM Cache'. Step 2 (Modify): An orange arrow labelled '2. Overwrite bytes 512..1023 in controller DRAM' merges the 512-byte application update into the cached 4 KiB block. Step 3 (Write): A red arrow labelled '3. Write modified 4 KiB sector back to media' flushes the 4,096 bytes back to disk. Metrics box below shows: 'Read count: 1, Write count: 1, Total operations: 2 (2x I/O magnification, latency spike)'. At the bottom, note: 'Check drive geometry with: lsblk -t (LOG-SEC=512, PHY-SEC=4096)'.
alt: A diagram comparing an aligned four-kilobyte write that takes a single operation against an unaligned 512-byte write on a 512e drive that forces a three-step read-modify-write cycle.
cap: On 512e drives, any write smaller than four kilobytes or unaligned to a physical sector boundary forces the controller into a read-modify-write cycle that doubles physical I/O.

name: p4-0112-fsck-passes
title: The Five Passes of e2fsck and Backup Superblock Recovery
spec: A two-part workflow diagram illustrating how e2fsck verifies filesystems and how to recover from primary superblock corruption. Left side: 'e2fsck 5-Pass Verification Pipeline'. Five stacked sequential rectangular stages: 'Pass 1: Checking Inodes, Blocks, and Sizes' (validates inode tables, extent trees, detects bad block pointers); 'Pass 2: Checking Directory Structure' (validates directory entries, checks '.' and '..' linkages); 'Pass 3: Checking Directory Connectivity' (verifies every directory links back to root inode 2); 'Pass 4: Checking Reference Counts' (verifies inode link counts; unreferenced orphan files are reconnected to '/lost+found/#<inode>'); 'Pass 5: Checking Group Summary Information' (reconciles block and inode allocation bitmaps against actual usage). Right side: 'Emergency Superblock Corruption Decision Tree'. Step 1 box: 'Mount fails: recovery required or invalid superblock'. Step 2 box: 'Run dry-run simulation: sudo mke2fs -n /dev/sdb1' (red warning: 'never omit -n, which simulates creation and prints backup locations'). Arrow leads to 'Discovered Backup Superblocks: 32768, 98304, 163840...'. Step 3 box: 'Execute repair targeting backup: sudo e2fsck -b 32768 /dev/sdb1'. Step 4 box: 'Primary superblock restored and filesystem mounted cleanly'.
alt: A workflow diagram showing the five sequential passes of e2fsck alongside the emergency recovery procedure using mke2fs dry runs and backup superblocks.
cap: The five verification passes of e2fsck validate filesystem consistency from inodes to bitmaps, while backup superblocks allow full recovery when primary metadata is corrupted.

name: p4-0112-quota-workflow
title: Linux Filesystem Quota Architecture and Six-Step Setup Workflow
spec: A two-panel technical illustration showing quota enforcement mechanics and the complete administrative lifecycle from Supercomputers for Linux SysAdmins Chapter 12. Top panel: 'Quota Limit Spectrum (Storage & Inode Axis)'. Horizontal timeline bar from 0 GB to 120 GB: 'Normal Usage Range (0 to 100 GB)' in green; at 100 GB marker: 'Soft Limit (bsoft=100G)'. When exceeded, a warning arrow shows 'Grace Period Timer starts (default 7 days: setquota -t)'. Between 100 GB and 120 GB: 'Grace Period Window (writes permitted, warnings logged)'. At 120 GB marker: 'Hard Limit (bhard=120G)'. Beyond 120 GB or after grace expiry: solid red wall labelled 'Hard Limit Exceeded: Write blocked immediately with ENOSPC'. Bottom panel: '6-Step Administrative Workflow'. Six numbered sequential workflow boxes: '1. /etc/fstab: add usrquota,grpquota to mount options (/dev/sda6 on /export)'; '2. sudo mount -o remount,ro /dev/sda6: freeze writes to prevent corrupt usage scan'; '3. sudo quotacheck -vugc /dev/sda6: scan disk and create aquota.user and aquota.group files'; '4. sudo mount /dev/sda6 (or remount,rw): restore read-write operation'; '5. sudo quotaon -va: activate kernel quota enforcement'; '6. sudo edquota / setquota & repquota -a: configure user/group limits and verify'. Callout on the right: 'NFS Export: start rpc.rquotad daemon on server so network clients can query repquota'.
alt: A diagram illustrating the quota enforcement spectrum between soft and hard limits alongside the six-step Linux quota administrative setup workflow.
cap: Quota enforcement uses soft limits with grace periods before hard rejection, requiring a six-step workflow from fstab configuration and read-only database generation to active enforcement.

name: p4-0115-sandbox-layers
title: systemd Sandboxing Layers and GPU DeviceAllow Pitfall
spec: Concentric rectangular layers depicting defense-in-depth isolation around a service process. Outermost boundary: Host Environment (root filesystem, /home, /dev, network namespace). First layer inward (Mount Namespace): ProtectSystem=strict (entire filesystem read-only except ReadWritePaths), ProtectHome=yes (hides /home and /root), and PrivateTmp=yes (allocates isolated tmpfs for /tmp). Second layer inward (Identity and Capabilities): DynamicUser=yes (transient unprivileged UID), NoNewPrivileges=yes (blocks setuid escalation), and CapabilityBoundingSet (drops raw capabilities, retaining e.g. CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE). Third layer inward (Devices and Syscalls): Seccomp box with SystemCallFilter=@system-service; adjacent Device Cgroup callout showing a red cross on PrivateDevices=yes (breaks GPU daemons by masking /dev/nvidia*) and a green check on DeviceAllow=/dev/nvidia0 rw and /dev/nvidiactl rw. Innermost core: Service Process running securely with restricted host exposure.
alt: Concentric boxes illustrate systemd sandboxing layers from filesystem and identity isolation to seccomp filtering, highlighting why GPU daemons require DeviceAllow instead of PrivateDevices.
cap: systemd sandboxing creates defense-in-depth isolation around services, but GPU workloads must avoid PrivateDevices and explicitly permit device nodes with DeviceAllow.

name: p4-0115-resolved-flow
title: systemd-resolved Architecture and DNS Resolution Path
anchor: ## 13. The other built-in services: networkd, resolved, timesyncd
spec: Flow diagram showing client DNS lookup paths through systemd-resolved to upstream nameservers. Top box: Client Application (calling getaddrinfo). Path 1: Libc consults /etc/nsswitch.conf with 'hosts: ... resolve [!UNAVAIL=return] dns' routing directly to systemd-resolved via D-Bus local IPC. Path 2: Legacy apps read /etc/resolv.conf, shown as a symlink pointing to /run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf, which defines 'nameserver 127.0.0.53'. Central component: systemd-resolved daemon containing three functional blocks: (1) Local Cache (configured with Cache=yes or no-negative), (2) Domain Routing Logic (evaluating Domains= search lists), and (3) Per-Interface Manager (ingesting link DNS from systemd-networkd .network files). Bottom egress arrows: Per-link queries dispatched over port 53 / DoT to Upstream DNS (e.g. cloud metadata resolver at 169.254.169.254 or corporate nameservers).
alt: A flowchart shows how client DNS lookups travel through nsswitch and the 127.0.0.53 stub listener into systemd-resolved, which checks local caches and routes queries to upstream nameservers.
cap: systemd-resolved handles DNS for applications through an NSS plugin or the 127.0.0.53 stub resolver, caching results and routing lookups to per-link upstream servers.

name: p4-0115-gpu-startup-contract
title: AI Node Startup Contract and GPU Service Dependency DAG
spec: Vertical dependency and ordering DAG showing the startup pipeline of an HGX GPU node. Top layer (Hardware & System Prep): sysinit.target and local-fs.target lead to network-online.target, alongside scratch mount units (/scratch with x-systemd.requires). Middle layer 1 (GPU Driver & Fabric): nvidia-persistenced.service (Type=forking) starts first; nvidia-fabricmanager.service (Type=forking) is ordered After=nvidia-persistenced.service. Middle layer 2 (Health Gate): gpu-health-check.service (Type=oneshot, RemainAfterExit=yes) runs after Fabric Manager, executing a readiness script (nvidia-smi -L count, nvlink status, ECC checks). Barrier line: Red stop line across the diagram showing schedulers blocked if health check fails. Bottom layer (Container & Cluster Daemons): containerd.service and kubelet.service ordered After=gpu-health-check.service and Requires=gpu-health-check.service; slurmd.service ordered After=munge.service and gpu-health-check.service; dcgm-exporter.service ordered After driver initialization. Workloads fan out inside kubepods.slice while host daemons stay protected in system.slice.
alt: A vertical dependency graph shows the startup pipeline of an AI node where driver daemons and a oneshot health gate must succeed before containerd, kubelet, and workloads start.
cap: A robust AI node startup contract uses drop-in dependencies and a oneshot health gate so container runtimes and schedulers only start after NVLink fabric initialization is verified.

name: p4-0116-host-logging-flow
title: Linux Host Logging Architecture and Data Flow
spec:
A three-tier horizontal layout depicting how log messages originate, get collected, and are dispatched on a modern Linux host.
Left column (Log Sources):
- Top box: 'Kernel Messages' (/dev/kmsg, ring buffer, drivers, OOM kills)
- Middle box: 'Systemd Services' (stdout and stderr captured directly by systemd)
- Bottom box: 'Applications and Utilities' (calls to syslog() writing to Unix datagram socket /dev/log; scripts calling logger)
Arrows from all three sources converge into the center column.
Center column (Collector: systemd-journald):
- Large box: 'systemd-journald'
- Inside callout 1: Attaches trusted kernel metadata (_PID, _UID, _COMM, _SYSTEMD_UNIT, _HOSTNAME) from socket credentials
- Downward arrow to storage box: 'Structured Binary Journal' (/var/log/journal/ persistent or /run/log/journal/ volatile)
- Local inspection arrow: 'journalctl' querying binary files with filters (-u, -b, -p, -S, -g, -o json)
- Rightward forwarding arrow: 'Forwarding Path' (via /run/systemd/journal/syslog or rsyslog imjournal plugin)
Right column (Legacy and Network Dispatch: rsyslog):
- Box: 'rsyslog Daemon' (evaluates facility.severity selectors such as auth.*, kern.*, *.emerg)
- Branch 1: Local text files (/var/log/syslog, /var/log/auth.log, /var/log/kern.log)
- Branch 2: Broadcast to logged-in users (:omusrmsg:*)
- Branch 3: Remote forwarder over network (@host:514 UDP or @@host:514 TCP with disk queue)
alt: Architecture of host logging showing kernel messages, service stdout and stderr, and syslog datagrams ingested by journald into structured binary storage, then queried with journalctl or forwarded to rsyslog for text files and network transmission.
cap: Figure 1.16.1b. Systemd-journald collects kernel messages, service output, and syslog socket datagrams into structured binary storage, optionally forwarding to rsyslog for text logging and network transmission.

name: p4-0117-zone-watermarks
title: Zone Watermarks and Page Reclaim Dynamics
spec: A vertical water-level gauge representing available free memory in a zone (Normal zone), marked with three horizontal threshold lines from top to bottom: high, low, and min. Above high: 'Normal Zone State' where free memory is plentiful and background kswapd sleeps. At high: marked as the hysteresis stop point where kswapd returns to sleep. Between high and low: allocations proceed smoothly without application stall. At low: annotated with 'kswapd wakes up'; an arrow shows kswapd scanning active/inactive LRU lists, dropping clean page cache and unmapping pages asynchronously in the background. The gap between low and high is labelled 'Spacing controlled by vm.watermark_scale_factor (default 10 = 0.1% RAM)'. At min: annotated with 'Direct Reclaim Threshold', derived from vm.min_free_kbytes. Below min: labelled 'Direct Reclaim Zone'; an allocating application thread is forced to synchronously reclaim memory (pgscand/s, allocstall), causing severe application latency spikes and high sys time. Bottom of the gauge: exhaustion below min triggers the OOM killer. A side panel contrasts the knobs: vm.min_free_kbytes sets the min baseline, while raising vm.watermark_scale_factor (e.g. to 50 or 100) widens the watermark gaps to start kswapd earlier and avoid direct-reclaim stalls.
alt: A vertical water-level gauge showing the high, low, and min memory zone watermarks, where kswapd reclaims in the background between low and high while dropping to min triggers synchronous direct reclaim stalls.
cap: Zone watermarks govern page reclaim: kswapd wakes at the low watermark to restore free pages to high in the background, while hitting the min watermark forces synchronous direct reclaim and latency spikes.

name: p4-0118-cfs-vs-eevdf
title: CFS Virtual Runtime Versus EEVDF Eligibility and Virtual Deadline
spec: Two side-by-side panels contrasting CFS and EEVDF scheduling mechanisms. Left panel: 'CFS (Linux 2.6.23 to 6.5) - Red-Black Tree by vruntime'. Shows an RB-Tree with nodes ordered by vruntime = actual_runtime * 1024 / weight. The leftmost node is selected: 'Always picks leftmost task (least vruntime)'. A callout shows a sleeping task waking up with an outdated low vruntime, immediately dominating the CPU and causing wake-up latency spikes for running tasks, necessitating complex wake-up heuristics. Right panel: 'EEVDF (Linux 6.6+) - Eligibility Filter and Virtual Deadline'. Shows the run queue virtual time line V. Step 1 Eligibility: tasks are partitioned into Eligible (vruntime <= V, have not received more than their fair share) and Ineligible (vruntime > V). Step 2 Deadline selection: among eligible tasks, the scheduler computes deadline d_i = v_i + (slice q_i / weight w_i) and picks the task with the earliest deadline. A latency-sensitive task requesting a small slice (q = 1 ms) gets an early deadline and preempts batch tasks (q = 8 ms) cleanly without heuristics.
alt: A side-by-side comparison of CFS selecting the leftmost task by virtual runtime versus EEVDF filtering eligible tasks and picking the earliest virtual deadline.
cap: CFS always picks the task with the lowest virtual runtime, whereas EEVDF filters for eligible tasks whose virtual runtime is below the queue average and selects the one with the earliest virtual deadline.

name: p4-0118-pstates-cstates
title: Active C0 P-States and Governors Versus Idle C-States Sleep Depth
spec: A two-part diagram illustrating active operating states versus idle sleep states. Top section: 'C0 Active State: P-States and Governors'. Shows a running CPU core executing instructions. A frequency scale shows the CPUFreq driver and governors: 'powersave' (dynamic lower clocks), 'schedutil' / 'ondemand' (load-responsive), 'performance' (pinned at max base clock), and 'turbo boost' (exceeding nominal clock when power and thermal budgets allow). Shows cpupower frequency-set -g performance and /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_governor. Bottom section: 'C-States: Idle Sleep Depths'. Horizontal progression showing C0 (active, 0 us wake-up latency, 100% power), C1 (halt, clock gated, ~1-2 us exit latency), C1E (enhanced halt, voltage reduced, ~5-10 us exit latency), and C6 (deep power down, caches flushed and core powered off, ~50-100+ us exit latency). A warning callout highlights that deep C-state exit latency introduces jitter for GPU completion interrupts and RDMA network polling, explained alongside the mitigation settings processor.max_cstate=1 and intel_idle.max_cstate=1.
alt: A diagram comparing active C0 P-state frequency governors and turbo boost against idle C-states showing the wake-up latency penalty of deeper sleep.
cap: Frequency governors and P-states operate only while the core is active in C0, while deeper idle C-states save power at the cost of tens of microseconds of wake-up latency jitter.

name: p4-0119-virtual-flavors
title: Spectrum of Virtualization: Language Environments vs HPC Containers vs Application Containers vs System Containers
spec: Four side-by-side vertical architectural columns comparing the isolation boundaries and mechanisms described in the text: 1. Column 1: Language-level Environment (Python venv, conda). Box shows host shell running activate script. Changes PATH, sys.path, and VIRTUAL_ENV. Label: Zero kernel isolation; shares host filesystem, PIDs, network, and real UID. Best for resolving conflicting Python packages on shared developer workstations. 2. Column 2: HPC Container (Enroot + Pyxis). Box shows Slurm srun --container-image unpacking an OCI image into a squashfs rootfs directory. Uses unprivileged user and mount namespaces without a daemon. Runs as the user's real host UID/GID so shared NFS/Lustre quotas and file permissions remain valid. Direct access to host GPU and InfiniBand devices. 3. Column 3: Application Container (Docker, Podman). Box shows single entrypoint application process inside full set of namespaces (mnt, pid, net, ipc, uts, cgroup). Isolated virtual network via veth pair or pod network; cgroups limit CPU and memory. Daemon (dockerd) or daemonless (Podman). Best for microservices and cloud-native AI inference pods. 4. Column 4: System Container (LXC, LXD, Incus). Box shows full init system (systemd) as PID 1 running multiple internal services, background daemons, and syslog inside a single container boundary. Feels like a lightweight VM with deep namespace isolation, but shares the host kernel. Bottom summary banner highlights key decision: choose Python venv for interpreter isolation, Enroot for multi-node Slurm storage compatibility, Docker/Podman for isolated service delivery, and LXC for multi-service environments.
alt: Comparison of language environments, HPC containers, application containers and system containers showing their isolation mechanisms and runtime models.
cap: From shell path overrides to full system containers, each flavor of virtualization trades kernel isolation depth against setup complexity and shared-storage compatibility.

name: p4-0123-training-path
title: The Full Distributed Training Data and Communication Path
spec: A wide multi-tier architecture diagram showing the entire path traversed by work in a distributed training step, as described in section 1. Arrange left to right in two aligned horizontal tracks: top track showing the Software Stack and bottom track showing the Hardware Infrastructure. Hop 1: Remote Data Store (Parallel FS / Object Storage, checkpoint store) connecting via Storage Fabric to Storage NIC. Hop 2: Network Filesystem Client (kernel NFS/Lustre driver) delivering raw shards to Host DRAM. Hop 3: CPU Data Pipeline (Python DataLoader workers, batching, tokenization, data augmentation) pinned to host NUMA node memory. Hop 4: Host-to-Device Transfer over PCIe Bus (PCIe Gen4/Gen5 x16 link, pinned memory / cudaHostAlloc) moving batches into GPU HBM. Hop 5: GPU Accelerator (SMs executing Forward & Backward passes, Tensor Cores, HBM memory). Hop 6: Intra-node Synchronization via NVLink / NVSwitch mesh connecting 8 GPUs on the same board. Hop 7: Inter-node Collective Fabric via Cluster NIC / InfiniBand HCA / RoCE over Leaf-Spine Network, driven by the NCCL collective library executing All-Reduce and All-to-All communication. Add callout badges highlighting potential bottlenecks at each hop: 'FS latency / metadata contention', 'Page cache eviction', 'Python GIL / CPU launch overhead', 'PCIe lane downgrading', 'SM occupancy / small kernel launch', 'NVLink error drops', and 'Fabric congestion / straggler rank'.
alt: A schematic of the complete hardware and software path traversed during a distributed training step from remote data store to inter-node collective fabric.
cap: A distributed training step traverses storage, host OS, PCIe, GPU accelerators, NVLink switches, and InfiniBand fabric, where any hop can become the bottleneck.

name: p4-0202-connection-model
title: State at the Edges versus State in the Network Core
spec: Two-panel horizontal comparison illustrating how link failure impacts connection state under two network models. Top panel: 'State in the Core (Circuit Switching / Virtual Circuits)'. On the left, Host A; in the center, intermediate Switch 1 and Switch 2, each maintaining an internal state table mapping [In-Port, Circuit ID] to [Out-Port, Circuit ID]; on the right, Host B. A red cross marks a link failure between Switch 1 and Switch 2. Callout text: 'Failure invalidates circuit state in transit; central controller or signaling protocol must tear down and re-establish each path before data resumes.' Bottom panel: 'State at the Edges (End-to-End Principle: IP Core with TCP/RDMA Edges)'. Left: Host A maintains endpoint connection state (TCP socket, seq/ack numbers, timers, congestion window). Center: Core Router 1, Router 2, Router 3, and Router 4 maintain only stateless destination prefix FIBs, holding zero flow state. Right: Host B maintains endpoint socket state. A red cross marks a link failure between Router 1 and Router 2. A green dashed arrow shows Router 1 instantly deflecting subsequent independent IP datagrams via Router 3 to Router 4. Callout text: 'Datagrams reroute dynamically around the broken link; connection state on Host A and Host B stays intact without notifying the core.' Bottom banner: 'End-to-End Principle: Keep core simple and connectionless; keep intelligence and state at the endpoints.'
alt: Comparison of a stateful core where link failures break circuit state against the end-to-end model where a stateless IP core reroutes datagrams while endpoints preserve connection state.
cap: In the end-to-end model, intermediate routers hold only prefix forwarding tables, allowing traffic to reroute around link failures without disrupting endpoint connection state.

name: p4-0203-switch-vs-route
title: Packet Transformation: Layer 2 Switching versus Layer 3 Routing
spec: A side-by-side comparison illustrating packet transformations, forwarding logic, and broadcast domain boundaries between an L2 switch and an L3 router. Left Panel: 'Layer 2 Switch (Same Subnet)'. Show Host A sending a frame to Host B. Ingress frame header: Destination MAC B (00:11:22:33:44:02), Source MAC A (00:11:22:33:44:01), EtherType 0x0800, IP Src 10.0.0.1, IP Dst 10.0.0.2, TTL 64, FCS. Switch inspects MAC table (FDB) only. Egress frame header out port 2: identical Destination MAC B, Source MAC A, TTL 64 untouched, payload unchanged. Dotted boundary indicates broadcast domain spans all ports; flooded broadcast (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff) crosses the switch. Right Panel: 'Layer 3 Router (Inter-Subnet)'. Host A sending to off-subnet Host C (192.168.1.5). Ingress frame header: Destination MAC is Router Ingress MAC eth0 (00:aa:bb:cc:dd:01), Source MAC A (00:11:22:33:44:01), IP Dst 192.168.1.5, TTL 64. Internal router flow in 3 callouts: (1) Strips incoming L2 header; (2) FIB lookup for destination IP 192.168.1.5 -> egress eth1; (3) Decrements TTL to 63 and recalculates IP checksum. Egress frame header on eth1: Destination MAC rewritten to Next-Hop MAC (00:55:66:77:88:99), Source MAC rewritten to Router Egress MAC eth1 (00:aa:bb:cc:dd:02), TTL decremented to 63, new FCS generated. Red solid boundary line indicates router drops L2 broadcasts, containing broadcast domains. Bottom summary box contrasts 3 dimensions: Addressing/Header (MAC preserved vs MAC rewritten and TTL decremented), Scaling (FDB flat per host vs FIB prefix aggregation), Broadcasts (flooded vs contained).
alt: Comparison of L2 switching preserving Ethernet headers and forwarding broadcasts versus L3 routing stripping L2 headers, decrementing TTL, rewriting MAC addresses, and terminating broadcast domains.
cap: An L2 switch forwards frames unchanged based on MAC lookup and floods broadcasts, whereas an L3 router terminates the L2 frame, decrements TTL, rewrites source and destination MACs, and confines broadcast domains.

name: p4-0205-routeget
title: Anatomy of an ip route get Kernel FIB Query
spec: Two-panel layout comparing synthetic query inputs with kernel FIB output anatomy. Left panel ('Simulated Query Inputs'): boxes showing Destination IP (8.8.8.8), Source IP ('from 10.100.0.45'), Input Interface ('iif lo'), and Firewall Mark ('mark 0x10'). Middle arrow through 'Kernel FIB Engine' indicating that the kernel runs the lookup rules and trie without sending wire packets. Right panel ('Output Anatomy'): the resulting line '10.30.7.8 via 10.20.0.254 dev eno1 src 10.20.0.45 uid 1000' with callout brackets pointing to: (1) matched gateway 'via 10.20.0.254', (2) egress interface 'dev eno1', (3) chosen source IP 'src 10.20.0.45' (critical for asymmetric routing debugging), and (4) socket context 'uid 1000'.
alt: Anatomy of an ip route get command showing how synthetic inputs like destination, source address, incoming interface and mark produce kernel-resolved next hop, device, and source IP.
cap: The ip route get command runs a full FIB lookup without sending traffic, exposing the selected gateway, egress device, and source address.

name: p4-0205-persistence
title: Ephemeral Kernel FIB vs Persistent Network Managers
spec: Two-layer diagram contrasting disk configuration with kernel memory. Top layer ('Disk Configuration Files'): boxes for Netplan YAML (/etc/netplan/60-routes.yaml), NetworkManager keyfiles (/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/), and systemd-networkd INI (/etc/systemd/network/*.network). Middle layer: 'Netlink AF_NETLINK (RTM_NEWROUTE)' socket. Bottom layer ('Linux Kernel RAM'): the Forwarding Information Base (FIB) containing active routes. A red dashed arrow shows manual command 'ip route add 10.30.0.0/16 via 10.20.0.254' writing straight into kernel RAM, tagged with a warning 'Lost on reboot or link restart'. A green solid arrow shows persistent daemons re-applying routes on boot from disk.
alt: Diagram comparing persistent configuration files in Netplan, NetworkManager, and systemd-networkd with ephemeral ip route add commands that disappear from the kernel FIB upon reboot.
cap: Routes added manually with ip route exist only in kernel RAM and vanish on reboot, whereas persistent managers reinstall routes from disk via Netlink during boot.

name: p4-0205-ipv6-linklocal
title: IPv6 Link-Local Gateway Scope Ambiguity
spec: Side-by-side comparison diagram. Left panel ('IPv4 Global/Subnet Gateway'): host with two NICs (eno1 on 10.20.0.0/24, ens1f0 on 10.100.0.0/24); adding 'via 10.20.0.254' allows the kernel to infer eno1 automatically because 10.20.0.254 falls inside a unique connected subnet. Right panel ('IPv6 Link-Local Gateway'): host with two NICs (eno1 and ens1f0), both sharing the fe80::/64 link-local scope; two upstream routers on both cables share or use link-local address fe80::1. A failure box shows 'ip -6 route add 2001:db8:200::/48 via fe80::1' rejected with 'Error: Device required for link-local nexthop'. A success box shows 'via fe80::1 dev eno1' explicitly binding the link-local next hop to the physical wire.
alt: Diagram contrasting unambiguous IPv4 next-hop gateway resolution with IPv6 link-local gateway ambiguity where fe80::1 exists on multiple interfaces and requires an explicit dev specification.
cap: Because every IPv6 interface shares the link-local fe80::/64 prefix, a next-hop gateway of fe80::1 is ambiguous without an explicit egress device.

name: p4-0206-marshaling
title: Transport Marshaling Grammars and Error Correction: Fixed, TLV, and Shared Dictionaries
anchor: ## 1. What a transport protocol must solve
spec: Two-panel comparison layout. Left panel: 'Digital Marshaling Grammars'. 1. 'Fixed-Length Fields (IPv4, Base TCP Header)': 20-byte grid showing [Src Port (16b) | Dst Port (16b)], [Seq Num (32b)], [Ack Num (32b)], [Offset (4b) | Flags (6b) | Win (16b)], [Checksum (16b) | Urgent (16b)]. Annotation: 'Parsed at fixed byte offsets with no loops; rigid, inflexible to evolve, wastes space if fields unneeded'. 2. 'Type-Length-Value / TLV (TCP Options, BGP Attributes, LLDP)': Sequence of tagged blocks: [Type: 1B (e.g. 0x02 MSS)] -> [Length: 1B (4B)] -> [Value: 2B (1460)], followed by [Type: 1B (0x03 WScale)] -> [Length: 1B (3B)] -> [Value: 1B (shift 7)]. Annotation: 'Self-describing and extensible via length-bounded loops; middleboxes can strip unknown tags'. 3. 'Shared Dictionary / Schemas (Protobuf/gRPC, ASN.1, YANG)': Box showing [Schema compiled out-of-band: message TensorMeta { int32 rank=1; string shape=2; }] -> Wire format: [Varint tag/wire-type] [packed binary bytes]. Annotation: 'Most compact and type-safe; requires both endpoints to share identical schema in advance'. Right panel: 'Error Correction: ARQ vs FEC'. Top flow: 'Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ)': Sender sends Segment 10 -> Dropped in transit (red X) -> Sender RTO timer expires or 3 dup ACKs arrive -> Sender retransmits Segment 10 -> Receiver sends ACK. Annotation: 'Zero constant overhead; costs 1+ RTT latency and requires sender timers and retransmission buffers'. Bottom flow: 'Forward Error Correction (FEC)': Sender calculates parity upfront. Transmits [Data Packet A] + [Data Packet B] + [Parity Packet P = A xor B]. Packet B is dropped in transit (red X) -> Receiver reconstructs Packet B using A and P without sender round-trip. Annotation: 'Zero recovery latency; imposes constant bandwidth overhead on every transmission'. Bottom callout: 'Addressing Modes: Unicast (1:1), Multicast (1:group via IGMP), Broadcast (1:all, IPv4 only), Anycast (1:nearest via BGP; mid-connection route shifts trigger TCP RST)'.
alt: Comparison of three marshaling grammars showing fixed-length headers, TLV option blocks, and shared dictionary schemas, alongside ARQ retransmission versus FEC forward error correction.
cap: Fixed-length fields parse at constant offsets, TLV allows modular options, and shared schemas minimize payload overhead, while ARQ exchanges latency for bandwidth efficiency compared to FEC.

name: p4-0206-transport-models
title: Transport Architecture Models: DoD, OSI, RINA, and Connection State
anchor: ## 2. Transport models: DoD, OSI, RINA, and connection-oriented versus connectionless
spec: Three-column architectural comparison layout. Left column: 'DoD (TCP/IP) vs. OSI Reference Model'. Stacked boxes showing mapping: DoD Application Layer (L7) maps to OSI Layer 7 (Application: HTTP, gRPC), Layer 6 (Presentation: TLS, Protobuf), and Layer 5 (Session: RPC framing). DoD Transport Layer (L4) maps to OSI Layer 4 (Transport: TCP, UDP, ports). DoD Internet Layer (L3) maps to OSI Layer 3 (Network: IP, ICMP, routing). DoD Link Layer (L1-L2) maps to OSI Layer 2 (Data Link: Ethernet, MAC) and Layer 1 (Physical: optics, copper). Center column: 'RINA (Recursive Internet Architecture)'. Shows a single repeating 'IPC (Inter-Process Communication) Layer' instantiated recursively at 4 scopes: Scope 1: Local Host IPC (between container processes); Scope 2: Rack / ToR Subnet; Scope 3: Data Center Fabric; Scope 4: Multi-region WAN. Each scope implements identical mechanisms: Naming/Addressing, Error Control (ARQ/FEC), Flow & Congestion Control, and Routing. Note: 'Layers are not distinct physics; they are recursive IPC blocks applied at different distance/failure scopes'. Right column: 'Connection-Oriented vs Connectionless Transport'. Top card: 'Connection-Oriented (TCP)': Shows shared state established prior to data: ISN negotiation, rwnd/cwnd tracking, RTT timers, socket buffers, TIME_WAIT state. Trade-offs: In-order reliable byte stream vs 1-3 RTT handshake setup latency, kernel socket memory overhead, conntrack table pressure. Bottom card: 'Connectionless (UDP)': Shows stateless 8-byte header (Src Port, Dst Port, Length, Checksum) followed directly by payload datagram. Trade-offs: Zero setup latency, zero kernel connection state, immune to conntrack timeouts; leaves ordering, congestion control, and loss recovery entirely to application (QUIC) or NIC hardware (RoCEv2).
alt: Diagram mapping the four DoD layers to the seven OSI layers and RINA recursive IPC scopes, contrasted with connection-oriented and connectionless state models.
cap: DoD and OSI describe protocol stacks while RINA models networking as recursive IPC at expanding scopes, reflecting the fundamental trade-off between TCP connection state and UDP stateless datagrams.

name: p4-0207-lab-topology
title: Namespace Testbed for UDP, Traceroute, and MTU Black Hole Lab
anchor: ## 8. Hands-on lab: UDP, ICMP, traceroute, and an MTU black hole
spec: A horizontal network topology diagram showing the disposable Linux VM testbed spanning 3 network namespaces (hA, r, hB) with the step-by-step experiment controls. Left box: Namespace 'hA' (Client Host) with veth interface 'vA' (10.1.0.2/24, MTU 1500, default route via 10.1.0.1). Inside hA, annotate test tools: 'nc -u', 'iperf3 -u -b 100M -l 1400', 'ping -M do -s 1472 10.2.0.2', and 'traceroute -n'. Middle box: Namespace 'r' (Router with ip_forward=1). Ingress interface 'rA' (10.1.0.1/24, MTU 1500) connected to vA. Egress interface 'rB' (10.2.0.1/24) where MTU is stepped down to 1400. In router 'r', highlight two fault injection points: (1) tc qdisc tbf rate 50mbit latency 50ms and netem loss 1%, and (2) iptables OUTPUT rule dropping icmp --icmp-type fragmentation-needed. Show an optional chained router 'r2' inserted between r and hB for the traceroute hop test. Right box: Namespace 'hB' (Server Host) with interface 'vB' (10.2.0.2/24, MTU 1500, default route via 10.2.0.1). Inside hB, annotate services: 'nc -u -l 5000' and 'iperf3 -s'. Illustrate the PMTU black hole packet flow: 1500-byte IP packet with DF=1 travels from hA to r, is discarded at rB because MTU is 1400, and when iptables drops the ICMP Type 3 Code 4 notification, the connection silently hangs.
alt: Network namespace topology for the hands-on lab showing client host hA, intermediate router r with MTU 1400 and iptables need-frag drop rule, and server host hB.
cap: Figure 2.7.18. The three-namespace lab topology implements an MTU mismatch and ICMP filter on router r to recreate and fix a Path MTU black hole.

name: p4-0208-local-resolver
title: Rack-level local caching resolver architecture and query routing
spec: A topology and request-routing diagram in three horizontal zones. Left zone (Cluster Nodes): two GPU worker nodes (gpu01 at 10.20.0.45 and gpu02 at 10.20.0.46) with their /etc/resolv.conf pointing to local rack resolvers (nameserver 10.20.0.10, nameserver 10.20.0.11). Middle zone (Site/Rack Resolver Tier): two redundant resolver boxes across distinct failure domains (Resolver 01 at 10.20.0.10, Resolver 02 at 10.20.0.11) running dnsmasq/Unbound. Inside Resolver 01, show three operational functional blocks: Block A 'Local Authoritative Records' loaded with domain=cluster.lab, local=/cluster.lab/, address=/gpu01.cluster.lab/10.20.0.45, host-record=gpu02.cluster.lab,10.20.0.46, and ptr-record=45.0.20.10.in-addr.arpa,gpu01.cluster.lab; Block B 'In-Memory Cache' storing recent external query answers with remaining TTL; Block C 'Upstream Forwarder' (configured with no-resolv, server=8.8.8.8 and cloud VPC resolver 169.254.169.254). Show three numbered query flows with distinct arrow styles: Flow 1 (green arrow) 'Local Cluster Query' for gpu01.cluster.lab or PTR 45.0.20.10 -> hits Block A directly -> answered authoritatively in sub-millisecond (less than 0.5 ms), zero WAN traffic; Flow 2 (blue arrow) 'Cached External Query' -> hits Block B -> sub-millisecond cached answer; Flow 3 (orange arrow) 'Cache Miss' -> routed through Block C upstream to Right zone. Right zone (Upstream & Observability): Upstream resolvers (8.8.8.8 / VPC resolver) answering uncached queries, and an Observability box monitoring Resolver 01 and 02 key metrics: query rate (QPS), p99 latency, SERVFAIL ratio, and cache hit rate (percentage).
alt: A rack caching resolver architecture showing redundant dnsmasq instances answering local records, caching external replies, and forwarding misses upstream to shield resolvers.
cap: A dedicated rack-level caching resolver serves local cluster records, caches external queries to reduce latency, and forwards cache misses upstream.

name: p4-0210-curl-timing
title: curl -w Connection Timing Waterfall and Stage Breakdown
spec:
A horizontal waterfall and timeline diagram illustrating the exact stages of an HTTPS request as measured by curl -w.
Top: A code banner displaying the exact command:
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'dns=%{time_namelookup} tcp=%{time_connect} tls=%{time_appconnect} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total} code=%{http_code}\n' https://api.example.com/
Middle: Horizontal timeline starting at 0.000s and progressing to the right with vertical checkpoint markers for the cumulative timestamps:
1. time_namelookup: end of DNS resolution (domain name to IP lookup).
2. time_connect: end of TCP 3-way handshake with remote host IP.
3. time_appconnect: end of TLS handshake (cipher negotiation, cert verification, key exchange).
4. time_starttransfer: first byte of HTTP response received (TTFB, time to first byte).
5. time_total: last byte received and transaction completed.
Bottom: Five colored horizontal duration bars (deltas) showing how each operational phase is derived from the timestamps:
- Phase 1: DNS Resolution = time_namelookup (Annotation: A long time points to DNS server latency or recursion).
- Phase 2: TCP Handshake = time_connect - time_namelookup (Annotation: 1 RTT to establish TCP connection).
- Phase 3: TLS Handshake = time_appconnect - time_connect (Annotation: 1 RTT for TLS 1.3 or 2 RTT for TLS 1.2 crypto exchange).
- Phase 4: Server Processing / Model Latency = time_starttransfer - time_appconnect (Annotation: Request travel, queueing, and model inference computation time before first token/byte).
- Phase 5: Content Transfer = time_total - time_starttransfer (Annotation: Response payload download over the network).
alt: A horizontal waterfall diagram showing the cumulative curl -w timing variables from time_namelookup to time_total with the five phase durations for DNS, TCP, TLS, server processing, and transfer.
cap: curl -w timing variables break an HTTP request into DNS, TCP, TLS, TTFB and transfer stages, pinpointing whether latency stems from network, crypto or model inference.

name: p4-0220-sse-buffering
title: Server-Sent Events streaming with proxy buffering enabled versus disabled in nginx
spec: Top-to-bottom comparative pipeline illustrating how nginx proxy buffering impacts real-time SSE token delivery. Top flow (proxy_buffering on, default): vLLM backend produces incremental token chunks (data: token text at 20 tokens/sec). Nginx receives small chunks but retains them in an internal memory buffer (proxy_buffer_size 4k). A buffer fill meter shows data accumulating (0.5 KB, 1.5 KB, 3.2 KB, 4.0 KB).
