A timeline next to the client socket indicates a 6-second blank freeze where perceived TTFT is severely elevated. Once the 4 KB threshold fills, nginx flushes the entire block at once, delivering a burst of 100 tokens all at once and ruining streaming ergonomics. Bottom flow (proxy_buffering off; proxy_cache off; grpc_buffer_size 4k;): vLLM emits token chunk T1. Nginx bypasses memory buffering and immediately writes chunk T1 to the client TCP socket. Client perceives immediate TTFT matching backend generation time (180 ms). Subsequent tokens T2, T3, T4 arrive continuously at steady inter-token intervals (~50 ms). Callout box highlights necessary directives: proxy_buffering off, proxy_cache off, proxy_http_version 1.1, proxy_set_header Connection empty string, and proxy_read_timeout 600s.
alt: Comparison of Server-Sent Events token streaming under nginx with proxy buffering enabled causing bursty delayed delivery versus proxy buffering disabled providing smooth real-time token delivery.
cap: Disabling proxy buffering in nginx ensures each generated LLM token chunk flushes immediately to the client socket instead of stalling until an internal 4 KB buffer fills.

name: p4-0220-prefix-cache-spill
title: Prefix-cache-aware routing with bounded-load spillover for LLM inference
spec: Flow diagram showing an L7 LLM router distributing prompt requests across three worker GPU replicas using prefix affinity and bounded-load spillover. On the left, incoming requests arrive: Request A and Request B share an identical 2,000-token system prompt prefix. At the center router, an affinity calculator hashes the prefix (hash(prefix) -> Worker 1). The router checks Worker 1 metrics: Queue depth = 2, KV-cache occupancy = 45%, which is well below the bounded load threshold (capped at 1.25x average cluster load, here 75%). Arrow shows Request A sent to Worker 1, which achieves an Automatic Prefix Caching HIT in GPU VRAM, bypassing the compute-heavy prefill phase and minimizing TTFT. On the right, a traffic surge scenario: Request C arrives with the same prefix, but Worker 1 is now overloaded with Queue depth = 14 and KV-cache occupancy = 88% (exceeding the 75% bounded load ceiling). The router's bounded-load rule intervenes: rather than exacerbating Worker 1's queue, the router spills Request C over to Worker 2 (Queue depth = 1, KV-cache = 30%). Worker 2 suffers a cache miss and computes the prefill, but starts execution immediately without queue starvation.
alt: Flow diagram of prefix-cache-aware routing directing matching prompt prefixes to the replica holding cached KV blocks unless its load exceeds the bounded threshold, triggering a spillover.
cap: Prefix-cache-aware routing hashes prompt prefixes to warm GPU replicas to eliminate prefill latency, using bounded-load spillover to prevent hot-spot overload.

name: p4-0226-byte-offsets
title: Anatomy of pcap-filter Byte-Offset Slicing and Bitmasks
spec: A two-panel technical diagram mapping pcap-filter byte-offset slicing to packet header fields. Top panel: IPv4 header byte grid (bytes 0 to 19). Highlight Byte 1 (ToS/Traffic Class) expanded into 8 bits: Bits 7-2 are DSCP (6 bits), Bits 1-0 are ECN (2 bits). Annotate filter 'ip[1] & 0xfc == 0xb8' showing mask 0xfc isolating DSCP EF (value 46 shifted left 2 = 184 = 0xb8), and filter 'ip[1] & 0x03 == 3' showing mask 0x03 isolating ECN CE (11b = 3). Highlight Bytes 6-7 (Flags and Fragment Offset, 16 bits = 'ip[6:2]') with filter 'ip[6:2] & 0x2000 != 0' pointing to bit 13 (More Fragments bit). Highlight Byte 8 (TTL) with filter 'ip[8] < 5'. Bottom panel: TCP header byte grid (bytes 0 to 19 relative to TCP header start). Highlight Byte 13 ('tcp[13]' or 'tcp[tcpflags]') expanded into 8 flag bits: CWR (bit 7), ECE (bit 6), URG (bit 5), ACK (bit 4), PSH (bit 3), RST (bit 2), SYN (bit 1), FIN (bit 0). Show filter 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-ack) == tcp-syn' with bitmask 0x12 (SYN+ACK) evaluated against 0x02 to match pure SYN packets without ACK. Include an offset shift callout box noting that placing 'vlan' in the filter shifts all subsequent IP/TCP byte offsets by +4 bytes.
alt: Diagram illustrating pcap-filter byte-offset slicing and bitmask operations across IPv4 and TCP headers for DSCP, ECN, fragmentation flags, TTL, and TCP flags.
cap: Byte-offset syntax slices specific protocol header bytes and applies bitmasks, letting captures isolate DSCP EF, ECN CE, low TTL, and pure SYN flags directly in the kernel.

name: p4-0301-cpython-exec
title: CPython Execution Pipeline from Source to PVM
spec: Flowchart diagram illustrating the two-stage CPython execution model and import caching. Left box: 'Source Code (script.py / module.py)'. Arrow 1 labeled 'Compiler (Frontend)' points to middle box 'Bytecode Generation'. Split path from Bytecode: Branch A (top) labeled 'If imported module' writes to disk box '__pycache__/module.cpython-312.pyc' and caches the module object in 'sys.modules'; Branch B (bottom) labeled 'If direct script' keeps bytecode in-memory only. Both paths converge with an arrow labeled 'Instruction stream' into a large right box 'Python Virtual Machine (PVM)'. Inside the PVM box: a cyclic loop shows 'Fetch instruction' -> 'Decode opcode' -> 'Execute against Evaluation Stack' -> 'Repeat'. Side callout at PVM: 'dis.dis() inspects bytecode instructions; runtime execution begins without separate link phase'.
alt: CPython execution pipeline showing source code compiled to bytecode, cached in pycache for imported modules, and executed inside the Python Virtual Machine loop.
cap: CPython compiles source code to bytecode on the fly, caches imported module bytecode in pycache and sys.modules, and executes instructions in the stack-based PVM.

name: p4-0301-refcount-cycle
title: Reference Counting Deallocation versus Cyclic Garbage Collection
spec: Two-panel comparison diagram illustrating CPython memory management. Panel 1 (left): 'Deterministic Reference Counting (Non-Cyclic)'. Box A: Object 'data = [1, 2, 3]' has an attached counter box 'refcount: 2'. Two labels 'a' and 'b' point to Box A with solid arrows. Step 1: 'del a' crosses out label 'a'; counter decrements to 'refcount: 1'. Step 2: 'del b' crosses out label 'b'; counter drops to 'refcount: 0'. Arrow labeled 'Immediate Free' leads to 'Memory reclaimed instantaneously'. Panel 2 (right): 'Cyclic Garbage Collection (Cycle Detector)'. Box X ('nodeA') holds attribute 'nodeA.peer' pointing to Box Y ('nodeB'). Box Y holds attribute 'nodeB.peer' pointing back to Box X. An external pointer 'root' is crossed out ('del root'). Both Box X and Box Y have 'refcount: 1' because they hold references to each other, yet zero outside references reach them. Dotted box labeled 'gc module (generational cyclic collector)' surrounds the isolated island with label: 'Periodic cycle detector detects unreachable group and reclaims memory'.
alt: Two panels comparing immediate deallocation when reference count reaches zero against circular references that require the generational cyclic garbage collector.
cap: CPython frees objects instantly when their reference count drops to zero, but requires the cyclic garbage collector to detect and break self-referencing reference cycles.

name: p4-0301-floor-trunc
title: Floor Division versus Truncation on Positive and Negative Quotients
spec: Horizontal number line diagram spanning from -4 to +3 with marked integer tick marks (-4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3). Two worked quotient scenarios are mapped above and below the line. Scenario 1 (Positive): true quotient 5 / 2 = 2.5 is marked with a diamond between 2 and 3. Above the line, two arrows point leftward to 2: green arrow '5 // 2, math.floor(2.5) -> 2 (rounds down toward -inf)' and blue arrow 'math.trunc(2.5), int(2.5) -> 2 (truncates toward 0)'. Callout: 'For positive numbers, floor and truncation agree'. Scenario 2 (Negative): true quotient 5 / -2 = -2.5 is marked with an amber diamond between -3 and -2. Blue arrow points rightward toward 0: 'math.trunc(-2.5), int(-2.5) -> -2 (truncates toward 0)'. Green arrow points leftward toward -inf: '5 // -2, math.floor(-2.5) -> -3 (rounds down toward -inf)'. Callout highlights: 'For negative results, floor division and truncation differ by 1'.
alt: Number line demonstrating that 5 divided by negative 2 yields negative 3 under floor division but negative 2 under truncation toward zero.
cap: Floor division rounds down toward negative infinity while truncation rounds toward zero, producing identical results for positive quotients but differing by one on negative quotients.

name: p4-0301-mutable-default
title: Mutable Default Argument State Leak across Function Invocations
spec: Two-row comparison diagram demonstrating the mutable default argument trap in service code. Top row: 'Buggy: def add_node(ip, nodes=[])'. Step 0 (Import time): function object 'add_node' is created in memory; its attribute '__defaults__' points to a single list object '[]' in heap memory. Step 1 (Call 1: add_node('10.0.0.1')): caller omits nodes argument; function appends '10.0.0.1' into the shared default list; returned value is ['10.0.0.1']. Step 2 (Call 2: add_node('10.0.0.2')): second request omits nodes argument; function accesses the SAME heap list, appending '10.0.0.2'; returned value is ['10.0.0.1', '10.0.0.2']. Red callout: 'State leaked across requests!'. Bottom row: 'Safe Idiom: def add_node_safe(ip, nodes=None)'. Step 0 (Import time): '__defaults__' points to immutable singleton 'None'. Step 1 (Call 1): 'if nodes is None' evaluates to True; fresh list L1 ['10.0.0.1'] is allocated. Step 2 (Call 2): fresh list L2 ['10.0.0.2'] is allocated. Green callout: 'Clean isolation across all calls'.
alt: Diagram comparing how a mutable default list retains appended items across subsequent function calls with the safe None-default idiom that allocates fresh lists.
cap: Default arguments evaluate once at module load time, causing a mutable list default to accumulate state across every subsequent function call unless None is used as a sentinel.

name: p4-0302-from-mutation-reload
title: Shared references, rebinding versus in-place mutation, and reload staleness
anchor: ### `import` versus `from`: shared references, cross-file mutation, and `reload()`
spec: A three-panel comparative architecture diagram showing variable binding, heap memory, and reload mechanics. Panel 1 (Rebinding vs Mutation): Box for share.py module namespace containing x -> int 1 and y -> list [1, 2] in heap memory. Downward arrows to importer namespace after 'from share import x, y': local x points to 1, local y points to [1, 2]. Show 'x = hack' breaking the local arrow and pointing to str 'hack' while share.x remains 1. Show 'y[0] = hack' modifying the shared list in-place to ['hack', 2], with red sync arrows showing both namespaces see the change. Show 'import share; share.x = 23' modifying share.py namespace directly. Panel 2 (Reload Staleness with changer.py): Top row shows changer v1 (message='First version', def printer). Importer A runs 'from changer import printer'; Importer B runs 'import changer'. Middle row shows changer edited to v2 (message='After editing'). Bottom row shows 'importlib.reload(changer)': changer.__dict__ is overwritten in-place with new code object. Importer B calling changer.printer() gets v2. Importer A calling printer() still points to orphaned v1 function in heap, highlighted with a red warning badge.
alt: A diagram comparing reference copying, local rebinding, in-place list mutation, and stale function references after a module reload.
cap: Rebinding a name imported with from stays local, in-place mutation affects all importers sharing the heap object, and reload leaves from-bound references pointing to stale functions.

name: p4-0302-transitive-reload
title: Shallow reload versus transitive dependency tree reload
anchor: ### Module introspection (`mydir.py`), dynamic string imports, and transitive reloaders (`reloadall.py`)
spec: A side-by-side comparison of shallow versus deep transitive reloading across an import graph ra -> rb -> rc. Left column (Standard importlib.reload(ra)): ra is reloaded; its internal 'import rb' statement evaluates against sys.modules where rb already exists, so rb and rc remain unchanged with stale flags on ra.rb.Y and ra.rb.rc.Z. Right column (transitive reloadall.py walker): flow diagram showing reloadall(ra). Step 1: inspect ra.__dict__.values(), filtering for types.ModuleType to discover rb. Step 2: check 'if rb not in visited: visited.add(rb)' to prevent circular loops. Step 3: call tryreload(rb) inside a defensive try/except block that guards unreloadable modules such as sys.monitoring. Step 4: recurse into rb, discover rc, reload rc. Bottom box contrasts the recursive reloadall2 (visited set) with reloadall3 explicit stack implementation using objects.pop() and objects.extend().
alt: A flowchart contrasting standard shallow reload which skips nested imports against a transitive walker that traverses module attributes with cycle detection.
cap: Standard reload updates only the target module, while transitive reloaders walk the module dictionary, guard against circular dependencies with a visited set, and refresh nested imports.

name: p4-0302-circular-imports
title: Execution timeline and sys.modules state during circular imports
anchor: ### Circular (`recursive`) imports: why `import recur1` fails while `import recur2` succeeds
spec: Two parallel step-by-step execution timelines side by side. Left timeline (import recur1 fails): Step 1: sys.modules['recur1'] created as empty module object. Step 2: recur1.py executes 'X = 1'. Step 3: recur1.py executes 'import recur2' (recur1 paused at line 2). Step 4: sys.modules['recur2'] created. Step 5: recur2.py executes 'from recur1 import X' (succeeds, X=1 exists). Step 6: recur2.py executes 'from recur1 import Y' (FAILS with ImportError: cannot import name Y from partially initialized module recur1, because line 3 Y = 2 has not run yet). Right timeline (import recur2 first succeeds): Step 1: sys.modules['recur2'] created. Step 2: recur2.py executes 'from recur1 import X'. Step 3: sys.modules['recur1'] created; recur1.py runs line 1 'X = 1', line 2 'import recur2' (instant no-op since recur2 is already in sys.modules), line 3 'Y = 2' runs to completion. Step 4: control returns to recur2.py; both X and Y now exist in recur1.__dict__, so 'from recur1 import Y' succeeds.
alt: A two-timeline diagram tracing module execution order and sys.modules registration to explain why import recur1 raises an ImportError while import recur2 succeeds.
cap: Modules register in sys.modules before running their body, so circular imports fail when a from statement requests an attribute before the source file has executed its assignment.

name: p4-0302-src-vs-flat-layout
title: Flat layout import pollution versus src layout build isolation
spec: A comparative layout diagram showing test runner behavior under two folder structures. Left panel (Flat layout: myops/myops/ and myops/tests/): Terminal executes 'pytest' from root directory /home/user/myops. sys.path[0] is set to '/home/user/myops'. The test runner directly discovers and imports './myops' from disk. Result: test passes (False Green), masking missing dependencies, broken build backend declarations in pyproject.toml, and missing package data. Right panel (Src layout: myops/src/myops/ and myops/tests/): Terminal executes 'pytest' from root /home/user/myops. sys.path[0] is '/home/user/myops'. Neither 'myops.py' nor directory 'myops/' exists directly in root. Direct 'import myops' raises ModuleNotFoundError. Arrow shows developer running 'pip install -e .' first: wheels and editable .pth are built, validating that pyproject.toml and hatchling package definitions work before tests can execute.
alt: A diagram comparing flat and src project layouts, showing how flat layout lets tests import local folders directly while src layout enforces packaging verification.
cap: The src layout prevents accidental imports from the working directory, ensuring tests run against an installed editable package and catching missing build metadata before CI passes.

name: p4-0303-callables-partial
title: First-Class Callables: Stateful __call__ Objects, functools.partial Binding, and operator Extractors
spec: Three horizontal panels contrasting first-class callable mechanisms. Panel 1 (Stateful Callable Object): Box representing 'RoundRobin' instance 'rr = RoundRobin(["gpu01", "gpu02"])'. Inside instance state: attribute '_hosts' pointing to list ["gpu01", "gpu02"], and '_index: 0'. Arrow shows calling 'rr()' triggers '__call__()' -> 'self.pick()', increments '_index' to 1 and returns '"gpu01"'. Second arrow shows next 'rr()' call returns '"gpu02"' and wraps '_index' back to 0. Label: 'callable(rr) == True'. Panel 2 (Partial Application Adapter): Box showing base function signature 'command(name, *args, user=None, **env)'. Arrow leads to 'functools.partial' wrapper object 'restart_nginx'. Internal inspected attributes shown in boxes: '.func -> command', '.args -> ("restart", "nginx")' (frozen positional arguments), and '.keywords -> {"user": "deploy"}' (frozen keyword arguments). Call trigger: caller runs 'restart_nginx(LANG="C")'. Splice box shows runtime merging: positionals ('restart', 'nginx') prepended to empty caller args, kwargs merged to {'user': 'deploy', 'LANG': 'C'}, passed to command(). Panel 3 (High-Speed Extractors with operator): Upper box shows 'Host = namedtuple("Host", "name gpus loc")' and 'Loc = namedtuple("Loc", "rack slot")'. An instance 'Host("gpu01", 8, Loc("r1", "04"))' is targeted by 'operator.attrgetter("name", "loc.rack")'. Arrows trace the dot-path traversal returning ('gpu01', 'r1') at C speed without creating a lambda frame. Lower box shows 'operator.itemgetter(1, 0)' extracting (item_1, item_0) directly by index.
alt: Three panels comparing a stateful RoundRobin callable object, a functools.partial argument wrapper, and operator dot-path accessors.
cap: RoundRobin encapsulates mutable index state inside a callable instance, partial freezes positional arguments and keywords into an immutable adapter, and operator accessors extract fields without lambda overhead.

name: p4-0303-itertools-mechanisms
title: Iterator Transformations: The groupby Consecutive Clustering Trap, pairwise Running Deltas, and batched Slices
spec: Three panels illustrating core itertools stream mechanisms and gotchas. Panel 1 (The groupby Consecutive Gotcha): Stream of node objects with racks. Top path (Unsorted Failure): Input stream [Node(g1, rack=r2), Node(g2, rack=r1), Node(g3, rack=r2)]. Arrows feed into 'itertools.groupby(stream, key=rack)'. Box shows state tracker: key 'r2' seen -> yields group ('r2', ['g1']); key switches to 'r1' -> yields group ('r1', ['g2']); key switches back to 'r2' -> yields duplicate group ('r2', ['g3']). Callout: 'Failure: 3 fragmented groups because groupby only clusters adjacent runs like Unix uniq!'. Bottom path (Sorted Fix): Input sorted first by rack key -> [Node(g2, rack=r1), Node(g1, rack=r2), Node(g3, rack=r2)]. Feeding into 'groupby' emits exactly 2 consolidated groups: ('r1', ['g2']) and ('r2', ['g1', 'g3']). Panel 2 (Sliding Deltas with pairwise): Input stream of monotonic counter samples: [1000, 1050, 1120, 1190]. 'pairwise()' sliding bracket shows overlapping pairs emitted: (1000, 1050), (1050, 1120), (1120, 1190). List comprehension '[b - a for a, b in pairwise(...)]' computes rates: [50, 70, 70] with zero index bookkeeping and constant memory. Panel 3 (Stream Batching with batched): Infinite generator stream of instance IDs passing through 'itertools.batched(stream, 100)'. Chunks of up to 100 items are emitted as tuples: Batch 1 (ids 1..100) -> 'client.bulk_delete(Batch 1)', Batch 2 (ids 101..200) -> 'client.bulk_delete(Batch 2)', Batch 3 (remaining 50 ids) -> 'client.bulk_delete(Batch 3)', respecting cloud API batch limits in O(1) space.
alt: Three panels contrasting the itertools.groupby consecutive grouping gotcha with pairwise sliding deltas and batched fixed-size chunks.
cap: itertools.groupby clusters only adjacent identical keys requiring a pre-sort step, while pairwise creates two-element overlapping sliding windows for rate calculation, and batched partitions streams into fixed API batch sizes.

name: p4-0304-polymorphism-pipeline
title: Stream Processor Polymorphism with Interchangeable Readers and Writers
spec: Layout diagram showing the processor(reader, converter, writer) stream architecture from left to right. Left block (Data Sources): Three subclass boxes inheriting from Reader: FileReader with read() reading local files, SocketReader with read() reading network sockets, and FtpReader with read() reading FTP streams. Middle block (Core Loop): processor(reader, converter, writer) containing steps: 1. data = reader.read() (break if empty), 2. data = converter(data), 3. writer.write(data). Right block (Data Sinks): Subclass boxes for FileWriter with write() and JsonWriter with write(). Below: Three call combinations from the text: processor(FileReader(...), converter, FileWriter(...)), processor(SocketReader(...), converter, FileWriter(...)), and processor(FtpReader(...), converter, JsonWriter(...)). Annotation shows that the processing loop relies solely on the polymorphic read() and write() interface without inspecting concrete object types.
alt: A stream processor pipeline where interchangeable FileReader, SocketReader and FtpReader inputs feed through a converter to FileWriter and JsonWriter outputs.
cap: Polymorphism allows processor() to orchestrate stream transfers across diverse sources and sinks through a uniform read and write contract.

name: p4-0304-namespace-dicts
title: Python Namespace Dictionaries and Pointer Links Under the Hood
anchor: ### Under the hood: namespaces are dictionaries
spec: Memory layout diagram showing four linked namespace dictionary objects and pointer references. Top level: object namespace root. Middle level: class rec namespace box containing __dict__: {'name': 'Pat', 'age': 40.5, 'jobs': ['dev', 'mgr'], 'method': uppername} and rec.__bases__ pointing to object. Bottom level: Two instance boxes. Left instance x box: x.__dict__: {'name': 'Sue'} and x.__class__ pointer pointing up to rec. Right instance y box: y.__dict__: {} (empty) and y.__class__ pointer pointing up to rec. Arrows trace two lookups: 1. x.name resolves directly in x.__dict__ ('Sue'). 2. x.age is missing in x.__dict__, follows x.__class__ pointer up to rec.__dict__, returning 40.5. A callout box contrasts x.__dict__['age'] which raises KeyError with x.age which succeeds via inheritance. Another box shows dynamic attachment rec.method = uppername, enabling x.method() and rec.method(x) to execute uppername(x) returning 'SUE'.
alt: Namespace dictionaries for class rec and instances x and y linked by class and bases pointers, contrasting direct dict indexing with dot inheritance lookup.
cap: Namespaces in Python are dictionaries linked by class pointers, which explains why direct dictionary indexing raises KeyError while dot lookup climbs the tree.

name: p4-0305-pathlib-anatomy
title: Anatomy of a pathlib.Path Object and Path Transformations
spec: A two-panel anatomy diagram detailing how pathlib.Path deconstructs file paths and transforms them without string manipulation. Top panel (Single Suffix): Displays the path '/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml' divided into highlighted segments. A bracket spanning '/etc/kubernetes/manifests' is labeled 'p.parent'. A bracket spanning 'kube-apiserver.yaml' is labeled 'p.name'. Within 'p.name', a sub-bracket spanning 'kube-apiserver' is labeled 'p.stem', and a sub-bracket spanning '.yaml' is labeled 'p.suffix'. Callout annotations show: 'p.suffixes -> [".yaml"]', 'p.with_suffix(".bak") -> /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.bak', 'p.parent.parent -> /etc/kubernetes', and 'p.relative_to("/etc") -> kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml'. Bottom panel (Archive with Multi-suffix): Displays 'q = Path("/data/checkpoints/weights.tar.gz")'. Annotated callouts show: 'q.name -> "weights.tar.gz"', 'q.stem -> "weights.tar" (drops only the final suffix)', 'q.suffix -> ".gz"', and 'q.suffixes -> [".tar", ".gz"]'. Side box: Key Path operations: 'Join: Path("/etc") / "kubernetes"', 'Checks: .exists(), .is_file(), .is_dir()', 'I/O: .read_text(encoding="utf-8"), .write_text(...)', and 'Glob: Path("/var/log").glob("*.log")'.
alt: An anatomy diagram showing how a pathlib Path object decomposes file paths into parent, name, stem, suffix, and suffixes for single and multi-dot filenames.
cap: A pathlib Path breaks file locations into structured attributes like parent, name, stem, and suffix, eliminating fragile string splitting and slash joins.

name: p4-0308-ratelimit-atomicfile
title: Token Bucket Rate Limiting and Atomic POSIX File Replacement
anchor: ### 3.5 Rate limits, concurrency and file operations
spec: Two side-by-side architectural diagrams. Left panel 'Outbound Rate Limiting (Token Bucket)': A bucket container labeled 'Capacity B tokens' has tokens dropping in from a tap at 'Refill rate: r tokens/sec'. Client requests enter from the top; when a token is present, a token is consumed and the request proceeds to the fleet endpoint with headers 'X-RateLimit-Remaining: N'. If the bucket is empty, the request queues or yields until the next token drops. An error branch shows HTTP 429 Too Many Requests leading to a pause respecting 'Retry-After: 30'. Right panel 'Atomic File Updates vs TOCTOU Race Condition': Upper bad path 'Unsafe Check-Then-Open' shows Step 1 'if exists(config.json)' followed by a time gap (window of vulnerability) where a concurrent agent or crash causes a race, resulting in 'Corrupted / Partial Read' or FileNotFoundError. Lower good path 'Atomic POSIX Replace' shows: Step 1 'Write full payload to temporary file in same directory (.config.json.tmp)' ensuring identical filesystem/mount point. Step 2 'Flush and close'. Step 3 'os.replace(.config.json.tmp, config.json)' executing an atomic directory inode pointer update. Step 4 'Mutual Exclusion' note highlighting 'fcntl.flock(fd, LOCK_EX)' and 'open with os.O_EXCL' preventing concurrent overwrite.
alt: A token bucket rate limiter handing out tokens alongside safe atomic file replacement using temporary files and os.replace compared to an unsafe TOCTOU race condition.
cap: Outbound rate limiting uses a token bucket to avoid 429 errors, while safe file state updates require writing to a sibling temporary file before an atomic os.replace.

name: p4-0309-transport-mocking
title: Transport Interception vs Client Method Mocking
spec: Diagram contrasting two approaches to testing HTTP clients. Top path (Bad/Brittle Mocking): Test -> calls client.get_json("/x") -> client.py calls httpx.Client.get() -> Mock replaces client.get -> skips URL building, header auth, query serialization, timeout configuration, and raise_for_status() handling. Returns dummy dict directly. Bottom path (Hermetic Transport Faking with respx / responses): Test -> calls client.get_json("/x") -> runs full client code: URL construction, query params serialization ('params={"limit": 2}'), header injection, retry logic, error handling -> httpx Transport Boundary / BaseTransport -> respx mock router intercepts the HTTP Request -> returns real HTTP Response (status 200, headers, JSON body with items [1, 2] and next_page_token 't') -> client decodes response normally. Annotate key takeaway: real client serialisation and parsing code runs end-to-end without touching physical network sockets.
alt: A diagram contrasting brittle client method mocking where client serialization is bypassed against transport-level interception where real HTTP request and response decoding code runs in full.
cap: Transport-level interception with respx or responses exercises URL formatting, header injection and status handling, whereas mocking client.get skips client internals entirely.

name: p4-0309-async-testing
title: Async Testing Anatomy and Cancellation Safety
spec: Anatomy flow of an async infrastructure test using pytest-asyncio and AsyncMock. Show three horizontal panels. Panel 1 (Test Harness): '@pytest.mark.asyncio' decorator -> 'async def test_worker_timeout()' -> wraps coroutine with 'asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout=2.0)' to guarantee test termination. Panel 2 (Collaborators & Injected Clock): Async client injected with 'AsyncMock(spec=ClusterClient)' -> 'mock.fetch_node_status = AsyncMock(return_value={"status": "ready"})' -> clock/sleep injected via fake event loop or 'asyncio.sleep' no-op replacement, completing simulated 60-second backoff in 0 ms. Panel 3 (Cancellation & Error Branches): Task cancellation flow: 'task = asyncio.create_task(coro)' -> 'task.cancel()' -> triggers 'try: await task except asyncio.CancelledError:' -> asserts cleanup logic (draining queues, releasing semaphores) runs before test exits.
alt: A three panel diagram showing pytest-asyncio execution with AsyncMock collaborators, bounded wait_for timeouts, and task cancellation handling.
cap: Async tests must be bounded with wait_for, isolate coroutines using AsyncMock, and explicitly verify CancelledError cleanup paths.

name: p4-0408-loop-register-results
title: Loop register structure and nested variable scoping
spec: Two-part diagram. Part A (Register in Loops): Left box shows a task running template on loop: [chrony, rsyslog, logrotate] with register: cfg_out. Middle shows three sequential execution iterations: iteration 1 (chrony -> changed: true, rc: 0), iteration 2 (rsyslog -> changed: false, rc: 0), iteration 3 (logrotate -> changed: true, rc: 0). Right box shows the resulting data structure cfg_out containing top-level key results: [ {item: 'chrony', changed: true, rc: 0}, {item: 'rsyslog', changed: false, rc: 0}, {item: 'logrotate', changed: true, rc: 0} ]. Callout annotations show Jinja filters: cfg_out.results | map(attribute='rc') yielding [0, 0, 0] and cfg_out.results | selectattr('failed') yielding []. Part B (Nested Loop Variable Scoping): Left column shows the collision trap where an outer loop over vhosts calls include_tasks with default item, and the included file also loops over [logs, public_http] with item, overwriting the outer vhost. Right column shows the fix using loop_control: { loop_var: vhost } on the outer loop so outer tasks use vhost.domain while inner tasks safely retain item.
alt: A diagram showing how Ansible loops populate a results array in registered variables and how loop_control loop_var prevents inner loops from overwriting outer loop items.
cap: Loops store per-iteration output inside a results list on the registered dictionary, and loop_control loop_var prevents inner nested loops from clobbering outer loop variables.

name: p4-0408-task-verdict-pipeline
title: Task evaluation pipeline: overriding failed_when, changed_when, and ignore_errors
spec: A three-stage horizontal decision pipeline showing how Ansible evaluates task results. Stage 1 (Raw Task Output): Box showing command execution returning rc, stdout, and stderr (e.g. grep -q 'Xid' returning rc=1 or tool returning rc=0 with ERROR in stdout). Stage 2 (Evaluation & Overrides): Two parallel evaluation lanes. Failure lane: default rule (rc != 0 means FAILED) splits into custom override branches. Branch 1: failed_when: xid.rc not in [0, 1] converts rc=1 into SUCCESS/OK. Branch 2: failed_when: "'ERROR' in out.stdout or out.rc != 0" catches error text and converts rc=0 into FAILED. Branch 3: ignore_errors: true catches failure but prevents host abort. Change lane: default module change detector overridden by changed_when: false to force OK status on read-only queries. Stage 3 (Play Recap & Flow): Boxes showing final status impacts: OK (recap ok=N, continues), CHANGED (recap changed=N, queues handlers), IGNORED (recap ignored=1, continues), and FAILED (recap failed=1, host removed from play with exit code 2).
alt: A decision pipeline showing how task exit codes and stdout are evaluated by default versus how failed_when, changed_when, and ignore_errors override host status and play recap.
cap: The task verdict pipeline shows how failed_when and changed_when override Ansible default exit-code evaluation and change detection before updating the play recap.

name: p4-0408-pause-vs-poll
title: Fixed pause versus active condition polling
spec: Two-lane timeline comparison diagram contrasting blind pause with dynamic until polling across fast and slow service scenarios. Top Lane (Blind Wait: pause: seconds=60): A 0s to 80s timeline. Fast scenario: service restarts and is healthy at T+2s, but Ansible blindly sleeps until T+60s, creating 58 seconds of wasted idle latency (highlighted with red hatching). Slow scenario: heavy GPU POST takes 65s to settle; pause expires at T+60s, next task checks port immediately, receives Connection Refused, and triggers a false-positive failure at T+61s. Bottom Lane (Active Polling: until: probe.status == 200, retries: 12, delay: 10): Fast scenario: probe 1 checks at T+10s, passes, and immediately advances the play, saving 50s. Slow scenario: probes at T=10s through 60s fail and retry automatically; probe at T=70s succeeds once the service finishes loading, proceeding cleanly without alert or failure.
alt: A two-lane timeline diagram contrasting the waste and failure modes of fixed pause 60 seconds against active until polling across fast and slow service restarts.
cap: Active polling with until and delay dynamically adapts to service readiness, avoiding the wasted latency and false failures caused by a blind pause.

name: p4-0409-dev-vs-prod-stack
title: Development versus Production Stack Architecture
anchor: ### Why production deployment is harder than `runserver` (*Ansible: Up and Running*, Chapters 6 and 7, `mezzanine.yml`)
spec:
Two-panel side-by-side comparison diagram contrasting a local development setup with the multi-tier production architecture described in the chapter text.
Left Panel: 'Developer Laptop (runserver)'
- Inbound: Browser on localhost:8000 (Plain HTTP, no TLS, no rate limit).
- Web & App Layer: Single foreground process 'python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000' (single-threaded, terminates on terminal exit, no supervisor, no concurrency).
- Storage Layer: Local file 'db.sqlite3' (file lock concurrency bottleneck, no network isolation).
- Caching: None.
- Secrets: Plaintext in settings.py.
Right Panel: 'Production Architecture (fleetapp / mezzanine)'
- Inbound Edge: Client requests over port 80 and port 443 with wildcard DNS (192.168.33.10.nip.io).
- Reverse Proxy (NGINX): Terminates HTTPS on port 443, redirects HTTP on 80 (301), serves /static/ directly, enforces rate limiting (limit_req zone=api rate=20r/s burst=40 nodelay).
- IPC Boundary: Connects via Unix domain socket (unix:{{ proj_path }}/gunicorn.sock) or HTTP upstream.
- App Server Tier: Process manager (systemd / Supervisor) managing Gunicorn/Uvicorn master and multiple workers ('workers = cpu_count() * 2'). Auto-restart on failure ('Restart=on-failure').
- Cache Tier: Memcached on 127.0.0.1:11211.
- Database Tier: Dedicated PostgreSQL instance, UTF8 encoding with template0 locale, SCRAM-SHA-256 authentication restricted to app host IPs.
- Secrets: Ansible Vault encrypted file (vault.yml) rendered with mode 0600.
alt: Side-by-side comparison of a single-process runserver stack with SQLite versus a multi-tier production stack with NGINX, Gunicorn, systemd, and PostgreSQL.
cap: Production separates edge TLS termination, multi-worker process supervision, and networked database concurrency that runserver compresses into a single local process.

name: p4-0409-nginx-ingress-pipeline
title: NGINX Edge Pipeline: TLS Termination, Rate Limiting, and Upstream Balancing
anchor: ## 6. The web tier: nginx, TLS and rate limiting
spec:
Top-to-bottom and left-to-right request flow pipeline based directly on nginx-site.conf.j2 and playbooks/web.yml.
1. Edge Entry Points:
   - Port 80 (HTTP): hits 'listen 80; server_name fleet.lab.example.com'. Arrow points immediately to 'return 301 https://$host$request_uri' (redirect branch exits).
   - Port 443 (HTTPS): hits 'listen 443 ssl http2'. Reads certificates 'fullchain.pem' and 'privkey.pem'. Enforces TLSv1.2/TLSv1.3 and injects Strict-Transport-Security header.
2. Routing and Inspection Layer (inside Port 443 block):
   - Branch A: 'location = /healthz' -> 'access_log off; return 200 ok' (bypasses upstream and rate limiting for load balancer probes).
   - Branch B: 'location /' -> enters Rate Limiter: 'limit_req zone=api burst=40 nodelay' backed by shared memory zone '$binary_remote_addr zone=api:10m rate=20r/s'.
     - Rate exceeded condition -> triggers HTTP 503 response.
     - Rate accepted -> forwards into proxy module.
3. Proxy Header Injection:
   - Injects 'Host: $host', 'X-Forwarded-For: $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for', 'X-Forwarded-Proto: $scheme', 'Connection: empty string' for HTTP 1.1 keepalive reuse.
   - Configures 'proxy_buffering off' for SSE/streaming passthrough and 'proxy_read_timeout 300s'.
4. Upstream Dispatch ('upstream fleetapp'):
   - Contains 'keepalive 32' connection pool.
   - Dynamically populated server targets with passive failure parameters: 'app01:8000 max_fails=2 fail_timeout=10s' and 'app02:8000 max_fails=2 fail_timeout=10s'.
alt: Flowchart showing NGINX handling port 80 redirects, port 443 TLS termination, rate limit checks, health checks, and upstream dispatch to application nodes.
cap: Inbound traffic is redirected or decrypted at the edge, passed through a token bucket rate limiter, and load-balanced across healthy application servers.

name: p4-0410-stat-assert-guard
title: Pairing stat and assert as a preflight guardrail
spec: Flow diagram contrasting early guardrail detection against downstream failure. Left box: Target file at /etc/nginx/conf. Step 1: ansible.builtin.stat queries target filesystem and populates dictionary 'st.stat' containing fields exists: true, isreg: true, isdir: false, pw_name: 'root', mode: '0644', size, checksum. Step 2: ansible.builtin.assert evaluates conditions [st.stat.exists, st.stat.isreg, st.stat.pw_name == 'root'] with quiet: true and fail_msg. Two diverging path panels below: Path A (With Guardrail) shows assert failing immediately at task 1 with explicit message 'Configuration file missing or owned by wrong user', playbook cleanly halts without modifying target. Path B (Without Guardrail) shows task 1 skipped or missing, task 2 applies template silently, task 3 fails downstream at systemd service restart with obscure error 'rc: 1 Job for nginx.service failed'.
alt: A diagram showing how ansible.builtin.stat extracts file attributes into a dictionary evaluated by ansible.builtin.assert, contrasting early guardrail failure against a cryptic service failure three tasks later.
cap: Pairing stat and assert creates a preflight guardrail that halts the play immediately with an explicit error message instead of failing downstream during service startup.

name: p4-0410-app-layer-triage
title: Triaging application failures: manual command versus Ansible execution
spec: Decision flowchart and environment comparison layout. Top node: Task fails at application layer (command or shell task returns non-zero rc). Action box: Extract exact command line from -vvv output. Decision node: Run command on target host by hand using 'sudo -u user -i'. Branch 1 (Fails manually): Root cause is in OS or host state. Diagnostic sub-boxes: check nvidia-smi for GPU state, verify missing shared libraries or packages, verify kernel modules loaded, verify file permissions. Branch 2 (Succeeds manually): Root cause is Ansible execution environment discrepancy. Comparison side-by-side callout: Left column 'Manual Login Shell (sudo -u user -i)' loads /etc/profile and ~/.bashrc, has full PATH (/usr/local/cuda/bin:/opt/slurm/bin:/usr/bin), active locale and proxy variables. Right column 'Ansible Task Execution' runs in non-interactive non-login shell, minimal default PATH (/usr/bin:/bin), stripped environment. Resolution: supply required variables explicitly using the task environment keyword.
alt: A decision tree and environment comparison showing how to triage application layer failures by reproducing commands manually in a login shell versus Ansible minimal non-login execution.
cap: Testing a failing command manually with sudo -u user -i isolates whether the failure stems from host state or from environment discrepancies such as minimal PATH in Ansible non-login shells.

name: p4-0501-lazy-pull
title: Traditional Pull vs Lazy Pulling with Remote Snapshotters
spec: Two horizontal sequential workflows comparing how a 20 GB PyTorch image starts on a cluster node. Workflow A (Top): 'Traditional Pull (containerd overlayfs)'. Step 1: Download all layer tarballs sequentially or in parallel over network (20 GB total; node network saturated, waiting 15-30 minutes). Step 2: Unpack tarballs sequentially into local rootfs snapshots on disk. Step 3: Launch container process PID 1 (GPUs sit completely idle until 100 percent of bytes are downloaded and unpacked). Workflow B (Bottom): 'Lazy Pulling (SOCI, eStargz, Nydus)'. Step 1: Download only metadata index and Table of Contents (approx 10 MB in 2 seconds). Step 2: Mount remote virtual filesystem immediately and launch PID 1 (container starts in under 5 seconds; GPU begins initialization). Step 3: Background and on-demand streaming: as PyTorch imports modules, only accessed chunks (approx 1.5 GB of actual code/libraries) are fetched via HTTP Range requests; unread compiler tools and debug symbols remain in the registry. A side callout box highlights: 'Eliminates GPU cold-start stall for large AI inference and training workloads.'
alt: Comparison between traditional image pull downloading all layers before startup and lazy pulling starting in seconds while streaming layer chunks on demand.
cap: Lazy-pulling snapshotters fetch index metadata first so the container starts immediately, downloading remaining layer data only as the application reads it.

name: p4-0501-registry-anatomy
title: Container Registry Anatomy and Multi-Region Replication
spec: Split diagram showing the three internal components of a container registry and how registries replicate across failure domains. Left Box: 'Registry Internal Architecture'. 1. Top tier: 'API and UI Server' implementing OCI Distribution API (endpoints: GET /v2/name/manifests/ref, GET /v2/name/blobs/digest, chunked blob upload, auth token verification). 2. Middle tier: 'Metadata Database' storing repository tags, RBAC policies, image vulnerability scan results, and manifest index mappings. 3. Bottom tier: 'Blob Store (S3, GCS, Ceph)' storing content-addressed immutable blobs under blobs/sha256/hash. Right Section: 'Topology Across Failure Domains'. Central Registry in Region A receives CI/CD build pushes. Directed replication arrows (push replication or webhook-triggered) sync images to Secondary Registry in Region B and an In-Cluster Registry/Cache in a Shared Services Cluster. Nodes in Region B pull from their local regional mirror rather than crossing the WAN, eliminating cross-region egress costs and surviving central registry outages.
alt: Anatomy of an OCI container registry showing its API server, metadata database, and blob store replicated across regional failure domains.
cap: A container registry splits metadata from content-addressed blob storage and replicates across regions to keep pull traffic local and fault-tolerant.

name: p4-0501-container-lifecycle
title: Container Lifecycle State Machine, Signals, and Exit Codes
spec: State machine diagram with four main state boxes: 'Created', 'Running', 'Paused', and 'Stopped / Exited', plus final garbage-collection state 'Removed'. Transitions and annotations: 1. Image to 'Created' via 'docker create' (rootfs assembled, namespaces set up, process not yet started). 2. 'Created' to 'Running' via 'docker start' (or directly via 'docker run'; PID 1 starts inside namespaces). 3. 'Running' to 'Paused' via 'docker pause' (cgroup freezer pauses processes); back to 'Running' via 'docker unpause'. 4. 'Running' to 'Stopped / Exited' shows four distinct paths: Path A: Clean exit (process finishes, exit code 0). Path B: Application error (exit code 1 or 2). Path C: Graceful stop via 'docker stop' (sends SIGTERM 15; if unhandled within default 10s grace period, kernel sends SIGKILL 9, resulting in exit code 143 or 137). Path D: Immediate termination via 'docker kill' (kernel SIGKILL 9, exit code 137) or Cgroup OOM kill (kernel OOM-killer fires when memory hits memory.max, exit code 137 with State.OOMKilled=true). Path E: Segmentation fault (SIGSEGV 11, exit code 139) or bus error from full /dev/shm (SIGBUS 7, exit code 135). 5. 'Stopped / Exited' to 'Removed' via 'docker rm' (writable overlayfs upper layer and container config deleted).
alt: State machine of container lifecycle showing transitions between Created, Running, Paused, and Stopped with commands, signals, and resulting exit codes.
cap: The container lifecycle moves through distinct kernel states driven by CLI commands, signal propagation, and cgroup resource enforcement.

name: p4-0503-controller-loop
title: Inside a Controller: Informers, WorkQueues, and Reconciliation
spec: Flow diagram showing how a controller inside kube-controller-manager reconciles state without hammering the API server. Left: kube-apiserver with box 'List & Watch API'. Arrow '1. Stream changes (events)' leads to 'Reflector' in the Controller. Reflector puts deltas into 'DeltaFIFO'. From DeltaFIFO, two arrows: one updates the local in-memory 'Indexer / Store Cache' (providing local fast reads), the other sends notifications to 'ResourceEventHandler (Add/Update/Delete)'. The handler enqueues only the object key (e.g. 'namespace/name') into a rate-limiting 'WorkQueue'. Right: 'Worker Goroutines' pull keys from the WorkQueue via 'reconcile()'. The reconcile loop reads current state from 'Indexer / Store Cache' and desired state from the object spec. If difference detected ('Drift'), arrow '2. Reconcile Action (POST/PUT/PATCH)' writes back to kube-apiserver. If operation fails with 409 Conflict or error, arrow returns the key to WorkQueue with exponential backoff.
alt: A controller uses a Reflector, DeltaFIFO, local Indexer cache, and rate-limiting WorkQueue to reconcile state and update the API server.
cap: Inside each controller: a Reflector watches kube-apiserver, updates a local in-memory cache, and pushes object keys to a WorkQueue for level-triggered reconciliation.

name: p4-0503-node-internals
title: Worker Node Anatomy: Daemons, Interfaces, and Hardware
spec: Structural node anatomy diagram showing all components running on a worker node. Outer box: 'Worker Node Host (Linux OS)'. Top layer: Host System Services running under systemd: 'kubelet' (listening on 10250, heartbeating via Lease to apiserver:6443, reading static manifests /etc/kubernetes/manifests), alongside 'containerd.service' and 'sshd / systemd-journald' (in system-reserved / kube-reserved cgroups). Middle layer: Plugin interfaces: kubelet connects to Container Runtime via 'CRI (gRPC unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock)', to Storage via 'CSI Drivers', and to Devices via 'Device Plugin API (/var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins/nvidia.sock)'. Also on host: 'kube-proxy' (or eBPF) programming host iptables/IPVS, and 'CNI Plugin daemon' (/opt/cni/bin, /etc/cni/net.d). Bottom layer: 'Pod Sandboxes and Containers' (cgroups, network namespaces) running user workloads and accessing GPU hardware.
alt: Worker node architecture showing the kubelet communicating with containerd over CRI, CSI storage, CNI networking, and GPU device plugins.
cap: A worker node combines the host kubelet systemd service with pluggable CRI, CNI, CSI, and device plugin interfaces that manage pods and hardware.

name: p4-0503-interfaces-grpc
title: Decoupling Through Interfaces: Kubelet and Pluggable Runtimes
spec: Component interaction diagram contrasting tight coupling with interface decoupling. Top: 'Kubelet (Core Kubernetes)' with standard method calls. Three vertical interface boundaries: 1. 'CRI (Container Runtime Interface)' over gRPC UNIX socket (calls like CreateContainerRequest, StartContainerRequest, RunPodSandbox) talking to either 'containerd' (via containerd-cri plugin) or 'CRI-O' or 'Firecracker', which in turn execute OCI runc/runw. 2. 'CNI (Container Network Interface)' invoked as binary plugin or daemon (ADD/DEL commands with JSON payload) talking to 'Calico / Cilium / Flannel' to attach veth pairs to host and pod network namespaces. 3. 'CSI (Container Storage Interface)' over gRPC UNIX socket (NodeStageVolume, NodePublishVolume) talking to 'Ceph / Cloud EBS / Lustre / local-path' to mount block devices into pod directories.
alt: The kubelet uses standard gRPC and binary interfaces to interact with pluggable CRI runtimes, CNI network drivers, and CSI storage systems.
cap: Kubernetes interfaces (CRI, CNI, CSI) separate the core kubelet logic from underlying container runtimes, network fabrics, and storage vendors.

name: p4-0505-etcd-topologies
title: Stacked vs Dedicated etcd Topologies
spec: Side-by-side comparison diagram of the two deployment topologies. Left panel: Stacked (Colocated) etcd (recommended for up to 50-200 worker nodes). Shows 3 Control Plane nodes (Control Plane Node 1, 2, 3). On each node: kube-apiserver process communicating via localhost:2379 to a colocated etcd pod managed as a static pod. Intra-etcd Raft peer communication connects the three etcd pods across nodes over port 2380. Pros and cons noted: lower cost, simple kubeadm setup, but shared CPU, RAM, and disk IO contention. Right panel: Dedicated (External) etcd (recommended for over 200 worker nodes and large AI/GPU clusters). Top row: 3-5 stateless Control Plane nodes running kube-apiserver behind a load balancer. Bottom row: 3 or 5 dedicated etcd nodes running on bare-metal or dedicated instances with local NVMe disks, isolated from control plane CPU and memory spikes. API servers connect to all etcd endpoints over HTTPS on port 2379; etcd members communicate over peer port 2380. High-latency cross-region links are marked with a red warning cross.
alt: A diagram comparing stacked etcd on shared control plane nodes against dedicated etcd running on separate NVMe machines.
cap: Stacked etcd simplifies small clusters, while dedicated etcd isolates disk and CPU contention for clusters with over 200 nodes.

name: p4-0505-registry-keyspace
title: The etcd /registry Key Hierarchy
spec: Tree diagram illustrating Kubernetes data layout in etcd under the root prefix /registry. Root node: /registry/. Branch 1: Core Namespaced Resources: /pods/[namespace]/[name], /configmaps/[namespace]/[name], /secrets/[namespace]/[name]. Note on secrets: stored as encrypted binary starting with prefix k8s:enc:... when EncryptionConfiguration is enabled. Branch 2: Leases: /leases/kube-node-lease/[node-name] (frequent node heartbeats) and /leases/kube-system/[leader-name] (controller-manager and scheduler leader election locks). Branch 3: Events: /events/[namespace]/[name] with a callout indicating high churn, 1-hour TTL, and redirect arrow showing --etcd-servers-overrides routing to a secondary etcd cluster. Branch 4: Custom Resources: /[crd-group]/[resource]/[namespace]/[name] (for example kueue.x-k8s.io or nvidia.com). Callout boxes highlight boundaries: 1.5 MiB maximum request size limit, Protobuf binary encoding, and anti-patterns (no metrics, no binary blobs, no continuous status updates).
alt: A hierarchical tree diagram of keys stored in etcd under the registry prefix showing namespaces, leases, events, and size limits.
cap: Kubernetes partitions cluster state under /registry, where high-churn events and node leases can be redirected or isolated from main state.

name: p4-0505-apiserver-ha-scaling
title: kube-apiserver High Availability and Scale-Out Architecture
spec: Architecture flow diagram showing scale-out control plane for large clusters (1,000 to 5,000 nodes). Left/Top: Ingress request sources: Worker Kubelets, Controllers (Kube-Controller-Manager, Kueue, Training Operator), Batch Schedulers, and kubectl clients. Layer 1: Layer 4/Layer 7 Load Balancer distributing requests. Annotation highlights: LB idle timeout must exceed API server watch timeout (min-request-timeout) to prevent mass watch disconnects and reconnect storms. Layer 2: Pool of 3 to 5 stateless kube-apiserver instances. Inside each API server box: independent in-memory Watch Cache (sized via --watch-cache-sizes=pods#5000), APF flow control queues, and etcd client pool. Layer 3: Storage backend split into two destinations: Main etcd cluster (3-5 NVMe members for /registry, pods, nodes, leases) and Secondary dedicated Events etcd cluster targeted via --etcd-servers-overrides=/events to absorb high-churn event writes without stalling WAL fsync on primary state.
alt: An architecture diagram showing a load balancer distributing traffic across stateless API servers with independent watch caches and split etcd clusters.
cap: Stateless API servers scale out behind a load balancer with long idle timeouts, offloading high-churn events to a separate etcd cluster.

name: p4-0506-endpointslice-readiness
title: EndpointSlice Controller Decoupling Readiness from Pod Lifecycle
spec: Three-column flow diagram showing how pod readiness affects EndpointSlices and traffic routing during an AI model load. Left column (Pod Lifecycle on GPU Node): Step 1 shows an inference container started; Step 2 shows Model Weight Loading where readiness probe fails with HTTP 503 while liveness probe passes with HTTP 200; Step 3 shows Weights Ready where readiness probe succeeds with HTTP 200. Middle column (EndpointSlice Controller Loop): Controller watches Pod conditions; at Step 2 it sets endpoints[0].conditions.ready=false and serving=false in the EndpointSlice object; at Step 3 it updates endpoints[0].conditions.ready=true and serving=true. Right column (Traffic Routing Plane): Service vllm-service backed by EndpointSlice; arrows show kube-proxy and cloud load balancers directing client inference requests only to endpoints where ready=true. Crucial visual callout emphasizes that unready pods drop traffic without being terminated by kubelet, distinguishing readiness from liveness.
alt: A three-column flow diagram showing how the EndpointSlice controller removes an unready inference pod from traffic routing during model loading without killing the container.
cap: The EndpointSlice controller updates endpoint conditions based on readiness probes, removing an unready model server from traffic while keeping its container alive.

name: p4-0506-status-conditions
title: Anatomy of Conditions, observedGeneration, and the /status Subresource
spec: Two-part diagram illustrating the status subresource boundary and condition structure. Top panel (Subresource Flow): An API client writes a spec update to /api/v1/namespaces/default/deployments/web, causing apiserver to increment metadata.generation from 1 to 2; the Deployment controller reconciles the changes and writes exclusively to the /status subresource, setting status.observedGeneration to 2 without re-incrementing metadata.generation, stopping infinite reconcile loops. Bottom panel (Condition Anatomy): Annotated breakdown of a single condition object inside status.conditions: type=Available (high-level capability), status=True (three-state value: True, False, Unknown), reason=MinimumReplicasAvailable (machine-readable CamelCase token), message=Deployment has minimum availability (human diagnostic text), lastTransitionTime=2025-05-10T12:00:00Z (timestamp updated only when status flips), and observedGeneration=2 (matching spec generation to confirm reconciliation is complete).
alt: Diagram showing the separation between metadata.generation and status.observedGeneration through the status subresource, alongside the six fields of a condition object.
cap: Writing status through the /status subresource updates observedGeneration and conditions without bumping metadata.generation, preventing reconcile loops.

name: p4-0507-job-restart-policy
title: Job failure behavior under restartPolicy: OnFailure versus Never
anchor: ### One-shot failures: restart policy and backoff
spec: Two side-by-side vertical panels contrasting how Kubernetes handles container failures in a Job. Left panel: restartPolicy: OnFailure. Top shows Job object 'oneshot'. Middle shows a single Pod 'oneshot-4nzfb' hosted on a Node. Inside the Pod, a container runs with args '--keygen-exit-code=1'. Container crashes with exit code 1. A curved arrow shows the local kubelet restarting the container in place inside the same Pod, applying exponential backoff (10s, 20s, 40s... up to 5m). Status badge reads 'CrashLoopBackOff (restarts: 4)'. Total Pod count remains 1. Right panel: restartPolicy: Never. Top shows Job object 'oneshot'. Middle shows Pod 1 'oneshot-1a2b' crashing with exit code 1. Kubelet does NOT restart it; Pod 1 is marked 'Error / Failed'. Job controller detects failure, decrements active count, and creates Pod 2 'oneshot-3c4d'. Pod 2 crashes and becomes 'Error'. Job controller creates Pod 3 'oneshot-5e6f'. An annotated callout shows cluster accumulating multiple terminated Pods in Error state, wasting etcd and pod table slots.
alt: Comparison between OnFailure restarting containers in-place and Never creating new pods that accumulate in Error state.
cap: Under OnFailure the kubelet restarts the container in the same pod with backoff, while Never causes the Job controller to spawn replacement pods leaving failed pods in the cluster.

name: p4-0507-work-queue-flow
title: Architecture of a parallel work queue Job draining items from a queue service
anchor: ### Work queues: parallel jobs that drain a queue
spec: Three horizontal stages showing work queue coordination. Left stage: Producer. A terminal box executes 'curl -X POST localhost:8080/memq/server/queues/keygen/enqueue -d work-item-N', pushing 100 items into the queue. Arrow points right to center stage. Center stage: Queue Server. A Kubernetes Service 'service-queue' (port 8080) fronts a ReplicaSet with 1 Pod running 'kuard' MemQ server. Inside the queue server, an array of 100 items ('work-item-0' to 'work-item-99') is shown with queue depth = 100. Right stage: Parallel Consumers. A Job 'consumers' with 'parallelism: 5' manages five worker pods ('consumers-0' through 'consumers-4'). Bi-directional arrows show each worker polling 'http://queue:8080/memq/server/queues/keygen' to dequeue an item, processing a key, and requesting the next item. When depth hits 0, workers receive empty responses, exit with return code 0, and the Job controller marks the batch complete.
alt: A curl producer pushes 100 items into a queue server behind a Kubernetes Service while five consumer Job pods pull items and exit upon drain.
cap: The queue pod decouples producer from consumers, allowing parallel Job worker pods to process items independently and wind down once the queue is empty.

name: p4-0507-gpu-node-sizing
title: Resource budgeting and cgroup memory allocation for an HGX 8-GPU node
anchor: ## 5. Sizing and placement guidelines for GPU workloads
spec: A full-node resource map representing an 8-GPU HGX server (e.g. 8x H100 80GB, 128 CPU cores, 1 TiB host RAM). Left column: Host Reservation. A top slice shows 'kube-reserved / system-reserved' allocating 8 CPU cores and 32 GiB RAM for OS, kubelet, and container runtime. Below it sits a DaemonSet slice ('dcgm-exporter') allocating 100m CPU and 128Mi RAM with SYS_ADMIN capability. Center column: Guaranteed Pod 'trainer-0'. Resource requests equal limits: 8 GPUs (all 8 devices claimed, preventing fragmenting), 64 CPU cores (matched to multi-worker DataLoader augmentation), and 800 GiB memory. Right column: Container Memory Cgroup breakdown (800 GiB total limit). A large block represents Process Heap and PyTorch pinned tensors (~736 GiB). A distinct highlighted sub-block shows '/dev/shm' backed by 'emptyDir: { medium: Memory, sizeLimit: 64Gi }' holding IPC and NCCL buffers, explicitly counted inside the 800 GiB limit to prevent OOMKilled exit 137. Attached volumes point into the pod: read-only dataset PVC at '/data', atomic checkpoint PVC at '/ckpt', and local NVMe scratch at '/work'.
alt: A diagram of an 8-GPU node showing kube-reserved headroom, a Guaranteed 8-GPU pod requesting full cores and RAM, and tmpfs shared memory budgeted inside the memory limit.
cap: Sizing a multi-GPU training pod as Guaranteed with requests matching limits prevents node fragmentation while budgeting tmpfs shared memory inside the container limit avoids unexpected OOM kills.

name: p4-0508-admission-scheduler-pipeline
title: Admission and Scheduling Pipeline from YAML to Node Binding
spec: Two-lane vertical flowchart illustrating control plane admission and scheduling. Left lane (kube-apiserver and etcd): 1. User/Controller sends Pod via 'kubectl apply'. 2. Authentication & Authorization verify credentials and RBAC. 3. Mutating Admission Webhook modifies spec: injects ServiceAccount token volume, DefaultTolerationSeconds, LimitRange defaults, sidecars. 4. Validating Admission runs schema validation, ResourceQuota checks, and PodSecurity enforcement. 5. Write to etcd: state is persisted as status.phase='Pending', spec.nodeName=''. Right lane (kube-scheduler): 6. Scheduler Queue picks pod. 7. Filtering (Predicates) checks: allocatable resources including nvidia.com/gpu, nodeSelector/affinity, taints and tolerations, volume topology and zones, host ports, pod topology spread. Decision fork: If 0 nodes pass, emit event 'FailedScheduling: 0/50 nodes available (20 Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu, 30 untolerated taint)' with PodScheduled=False. 8. Scoring (Priorities) ranks passing nodes: pod spread, image locality, resource balance, affinity weights. 9. Reserve & Permit (gang scheduling check). 10. Binding: scheduler sends POST Binding to apiserver, setting spec.nodeName, emitting event 'Scheduled: Successfully assigned ns/pod to node' and PodScheduled=True.
alt: A step-by-step pipeline from kubectl apply through API server admission and etcd storage to the scheduler filter, score, and binding stages.
cap: The control-plane pipeline authenticates and mutates the pod, persists it with an empty nodeName, and filters and scores candidate nodes before posting the binding.

name: p4-0509-kubeletconfig-blocks
title: Anatomy of a Production GPU KubeletConfiguration
anchor: ## 2. A production KubeletConfiguration for GPU nodes
spec: Diagram showing the functional blocks of the KubeletConfiguration YAML file laid out side by side or in stacked logical groups. Group 1: Authentication & Authorization (anonymous.enabled: false, webhook.enabled: true, authorization.mode: Webhook, serverTLSBootstrap: true). Group 2: Host & Runtime Hardening (cgroupDriver: systemd, cgroupsPerQOS: true, protectKernelDefaults: true with checked sysctls vm.overcommit_memory=1 and panic settings, seccompDefault: true). Group 3: Scale & Pull Control (maxPods: 110, podPidsLimit: 8192, serializeImagePulls: false, maxParallelImagePulls: 3, registryPullQPS: 20). Group 4: AI/GPU Resource & NUMA Management (cpuManagerPolicy: static, full-pcpus-only: true, reservedSystemCPUs: 0-3, memoryManagerPolicy: Static, topologyManagerPolicy: single-numa-node, topologyManagerScope: pod). Group 5: Reservations & Node Allocatable (kubeReserved: 4Gi/5Gi, systemReserved: 8Gi/5Gi, enforceNodeAllocatable: [pods]). Group 6: Node-Pressure Eviction Thresholds (evictionHard memory.available: 2Gi, evictionSoft memory.available: 4Gi over 2m, evictionMinimumReclaim: 1Gi). Annotations indicate why each block matters for AI inference/training nodes.
alt: Functional decomposition of the production GPU KubeletConfiguration into six key operational blocks from security and hardening to NUMA topology and eviction.
cap: A production KubeletConfiguration organizes node parameters into six key operational domains for GPU stability and performance.

name: p4-0509-node-allocatable-math
title: Calculating Node Allocatable from Raw Capacity
spec: A horizontal or stacked bar chart illustrating the allocation math. Left: Total Node Capacity bar (e.g., CPU, Memory, Ephemeral Storage). Minus kube-reserved bracket (for kubelet, containerd, node problem detector; e.g. 4Gi RAM, cores 0-3). Minus system-reserved bracket (for sshd, systemd, udev, OS daemons; e.g. 8Gi RAM). Minus eviction-threshold bracket (hard eviction threshold reserve e.g. 2Gi RAM). Equals Allocatable bar on the right. Below Allocatable, show how the Kubernetes Scheduler views the node: Pod Requests must fit entirely inside Allocatable. Show 'Allocated Resources' as the sum of current pod requests/limits within Allocatable, highlighting that raw Capacity is never what the scheduler sees. Show enforceNodeAllocatable boundary around the pods cgroup.
alt: Breakdown of raw node capacity minus kube-reserved, system-reserved, and eviction thresholds to produce node allocatable used by the scheduler.
cap: Node Allocatable is derived by subtracting kube-reserved, system-reserved, and eviction thresholds from raw node capacity.

name: p4-0509-qos-comparison-matrix
title: QoS Classes: Cgroups, Requests, OOM Scores, and Eviction Priority
spec: A comparison table/matrix layout across the three QoS classes: Guaranteed, Burstable, and BestEffort. Show columns: 1. QoS Class; 2. Request/Limit Criteria (Guaranteed: requests == limits for all containers; Burstable: at least one request or limit set, requests < limits; BestEffort: no requests or limits set); 3. Cgroup Location (Guaranteed: /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-pod<uid>.slice; Burstable: .../kubepods-burstable.slice/...; BestEffort: .../kubepods-besteffort.slice/...); 4. Linux Kernel oom_score_adj (Guaranteed: -997; Burstable: calculated proportional between -998 and 1000; BestEffort: 1000; kubelet/runtime processes: -999); 5. Eviction Order under Node Memory Pressure (Guaranteed: Tier 2, evicted last only if system daemons exceed reserved; Burstable: Tier 1 if usage > request ranked by priority then excess bytes, Tier 2 if usage <= request; BestEffort: Tier 1, evicted first because request is 0).
alt: Comparison of Guaranteed, Burstable, and BestEffort QoS classes across cgroup paths, resource requests, oom scores, and eviction ranks.
cap: The three QoS classes determine cgroup placement, kernel OOM scores, and the kubelet's eviction ranking under pressure.

name: p4-0509-probe-decision-flow
title: Probe Architecture and Decision Flowchart
spec: Flowchart tracing how kubelet executes probes on a pod container over its lifecycle. Step 1: Container starts. Decision: Is startupProbe defined? If Yes, poll startupProbe (/healthz, period 10s, failureThreshold 30 = up to 300s window). While failing and attempts < threshold: keep waiting, do NOT run liveness or readiness probes. If startup probe reaches failureThreshold: trigger container kill and restart per restartPolicy. If startup probe succeeds (or none defined): proceed to parallel monitoring. Branch A: readinessProbe (/ready, period 5s, timeout 3s). Check: is model loaded and internal worker ready to accept traffic? If No: mark Pod NotReady, remove Pod IP from Service endpoints (no container restart). If Yes: Pod Ready, add to Service endpoints. Note: Never check hard external dependencies (e.g. database) that would cascade failure. Branch B: livenessProbe (/healthz, period 10s, timeout 3s). Check: is container process internally deadlocked/hung? If fails consecutive failureThreshold times: kill container and restart per restartPolicy.
alt: Decision flowchart detailing startup probe gating, readiness probe endpoint detachment, and liveness probe restart loops.
cap: Startup probes gate execution until initialization completes, while readiness and liveness probes independently govern service traffic and process restarts.

name: p4-0509-kubelet-observability-pipeline
title: Kubelet Observability and Metric Pipeline
spec: Architecture diagram illustrating the kubelet observability components and exported metric streams. Center: Kubelet core daemon on port :10250. Inputs on the node: cAdvisor subsystem reading cgroup v2 stats (/sys/fs/cgroup), CRI runtime events from containerd, prober execution engine running http/tcp/exec checks, and PLEG (Pod Lifecycle Event Generator) watching relist events. Exporters/endpoints shown radiating from kubelet: 1. :10250/metrics (kubelet_running_pods, kubelet_running_containers, kubelet_pleg_relist_duration_seconds, kubelet_pleg_relist_interval_seconds, kubelet_evictions, kubelet_pod_start_duration_seconds, kubelet_certificate_manager_client_ttl_seconds). 2. :10250/metrics/cadvisor (container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total, container_memory_working_set_bytes, container_oom_events_total). 3. :10250/metrics/probes (prober_probe_total). Callouts highlight critical alerting conditions: PLEG relist > 3s, client cert TTL < 7d, CFS throttling ratio > 20% on latency-critical workloads, and memory.available approaching evictionHard.
alt: Architecture diagram of the kubelet metrics engine gathering data from cAdvisor, CRI, probes, and PLEG and exposing them on port 10250.
cap: The kubelet gathers container, cgroup, probe, and lifecycle telemetry to expose distinct metric endpoints on port 10250.

name: p4-0509-troubleshooting-flowchart
title: Kubelet and Node Failure Triage Tree
spec: Triage decision tree for node-level failures. Root: Node or Pod anomaly detected. Branch 1: Node status = NotReady. Check systemctl status kubelet. If stopped: check journalctl for swap on, cgroup driver mismatch, protectKernelDefaults failure, or stale cpu_manager_state. If running: check kube-node-lease expiry, network partition to apiserver, or container runtime health (crictl info). Branch 2: Pods failing / restarting. Sub-branch A: Pod Last State = Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code 137. Cause: Container memory limit reached cgroup ceiling (memory.max). Check memory.events and working set. Sub-branch B: Pod Status = Failed, Reason: Evicted. Message: 'The node was low on resource: memory/nodefs'. Cause: Node-pressure eviction manager triggered before OOM killer. Check memory.available vs evictionHard. Sub-branch C: Pod Unhealthy / Probe failures. Cause: CFS throttling delaying HTTP probe > timeoutSeconds, or NetworkPolicy blocking node-to-pod probe traffic. Sub-branch D: TopologyAffinityError. Cause: TopologyManager single-numa-node cannot fit requested GPUs/CPUs on one NUMA node.
alt: Triage flowchart mapping node NotReady, OOMKilled, Evicted, probe failure, and TopologyAffinityError symptoms to root causes and inspection commands.
cap: A diagnostic decision tree resolves common node failures by separating kubelet crashes, cgroup OOM kills, node-pressure evictions, and NUMA admission errors.

name: p4-0510-socket-lb
title: Socket-Level Load Balancing with eBPF vs Traditional Packet DNAT
anchor: ### eBPF replacements (Cilium kube-proxy replacement, Calico eBPF dataplane)
spec: Two-panel vertical comparison. Top panel: Traditional kube-proxy packet DNAT. Step 1: Application in Pod calls connect() to ClusterIP:80 (10.96.0.100:80). Step 2: Linux kernel constructs TCP SYN packet with src=10.244.1.5, dst=10.96.0.100:80. Step 3: Packet leaves Pod veth and hits netfilter PREROUTING hook on host. Step 4: iptables or nftables DNAT rewrites destination IP:port to Pod IP 10.244.2.9:8000 and allocates a conntrack entry. Step 5: Reverse NAT is required on return packet path. Bottom panel: Cilium eBPF Socket-LB (cgroup/connect4). Step 1: Application calls connect() to ClusterIP:80. Step 2: Attached eBPF cgroup/connect4 hook intercepts the syscall inside the kernel before packet construction. Step 3: Hook queries BPF LB map and directly rewrites the destination sockaddr_in to 10.244.2.9:8000 in memory. Step 4: Kernel constructs TCP SYN packet with dst=10.244.2.9:8000 already populated. Step 5: Wire packet flows directly to target pod with zero netfilter DNAT, zero conntrack allocation, and no reverse NAT.
alt: A comparison showing traditional packet DNAT allocating conntrack entries in netfilter hooks versus Cilium eBPF translating destination sockaddr inside the socket connect hook before packet generation.
cap: eBPF socket load balancing rewrites the destination sockaddr inside the cgroup connect4 hook before packets are built, bypassing netfilter DNAT and conntrack entirely.

name: p4-0510-metallb-l2-vs-bgp
title: Bare-Metal Load Balancing: MetalLB Layer 2 Mode vs BGP ECMP Mode
spec: Two-column comparison showing bare-metal LoadBalancer routing. Left column: Layer 2 Mode (L2Advertisement). External VIP 198.51.100.1. A single elected speaker node (Node 1) answers ARP/NDP requests for the VIP on the LAN. All external ingress traffic flows into Node 1 interface eth0, creating a single-node bandwidth bottleneck. Node 1 then forwards via kube-proxy or overlay to backend pods on Node 2 and Node 3. Right column: BGP Mode (BGPAdvertisement). External VIP 198.51.100.1. All speaker nodes (Node 1, Node 2, Node 3) establish BGP peering sessions over TCP port 179 with Top-of-Rack (ToR) physical switches. Each node advertises a /32 route to the VIP. ToR switch performs line-rate ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path) hashing, distributing incoming connections evenly across all nodes without a single-node choke point.
alt: A diagram comparing MetalLB Layer 2 mode with a single elected ARP speaker node against BGP mode where all nodes peer with the top of rack switch for multi-node ECMP.
cap: MetalLB Layer 2 mode funnels all ingress traffic through one elected ARP speaker node, while BGP mode peers directly with rack switches for line-rate ECMP load balancing.

name: p4-0510-hairpin-masq
title: Hairpin NAT Deadlock and KUBE-MARK-MASQ Resolution
spec: Two-panel sequence illustrating hairpin traffic. Top panel: Broken flow without MASQUERADE. Pod A (IP 10.244.1.5) sends a request to its own Service VIP (10.96.0.100:80). Host DNAT rewrites the destination back to Pod A itself (10.244.1.5:8000). The packet arrives at Pod A with src=10.244.1.5 and dst=10.244.1.5. Pod A kernel sees source is local to its network namespace and responds directly via loopback (lo) interface rather than eth0. Host conntrack is bypassed, the reply is never un-DNATed back to VIP, and Pod A socket hangs indefinitely. Bottom panel: Hairpin resolution with KUBE-MARK-MASQ. Hairpin packet matches rule -s 10.244.1.5 in KUBE-SEP chain, receiving mark 0x4000. POSTROUTING rule masquerades the source IP to node/bridge IP (10.244.1.1). Packet arrives at Pod A with src=10.244.1.1, dst=10.244.1.5. Reply SYN-ACK must route back through host veth/bridge to reach 10.244.1.1, allowing host conntrack to reverse both DNAT and SNAT correctly.
alt: A diagram showing how a pod sending traffic to its own Service VIP deadlocks via loopback delivery unless KUBE-MARK-MASQ forces source NAT through the host bridge.
cap: Hairpin traffic deadlocks when a pod replies to itself over loopback unless KUBE-MARK-MASQ applies source NAT so replies route through host conntrack.

name: p4-0511-cpa-autoscaling
title: Proactive Cluster-Proportional Autoscaler vs Reactive HPA During Job Launch Bursts
spec: Side-by-side comparison layout showing how CoreDNS handles a sudden 5,000-pod job startup under two autoscaling models. Left panel: 'Reactive CPU-based HPA'. Step 1: 5,000 training pods launch simultaneously; query rate immediately surges to 100k+ QPS due to pod count × lookup rate × ndots:5 amplification. Step 2: The default 2 CoreDNS pods (handling 10k-20k QPS/core) saturate immediately, suffering CPU throttling and packet drops. Step 3: HPA evaluation metric lags behind by 15-60 seconds; pods experience 5s timeouts and startup crashes before extra replicas become Ready. Right panel: 'Proactive Cluster-Proportional Autoscaler (CPA)'. Step 1: CPA watches cluster size (nodesPerReplica: 16, coresPerReplica: 256, min: 3). As cluster scales up to 1,000 GPU nodes ahead of the run, CPA scales CoreDNS to 63 replicas before pods start. Step 2: Pod anti-affinity spreads replicas across nodes/zones; PodDisruptionBudget (minAvailable: 50%) protects availability; system-cluster-critical priority prevents eviction. Step 3: 5,000 pods launch and the 100k+ QPS burst distributes across the pre-warmed pool without latency spikes or drops.
alt: A comparison shows how reactive HPA causes query drops during sudden pod start bursts while cluster-proportional autoscaling provisions CoreDNS replicas ahead of time based on node and core counts.
cap: Cluster-proportional autoscaling sizes CoreDNS replicas before a large job launches, avoiding the scaling lag and query drops of reactive CPU autoscalers.

name: p4-0511-dns-tcp-truncation
title: DNS UDP Truncation (TC Bit) and TCP/53 Fallback Under Default-Deny NetworkPolicy
spec: Sequence and decision flow showing how large DNS responses fall back to TCP/53 and fail when egress NetworkPolicies only permit UDP. Top swimlane shows 'Pod (Client Resolver)', middle swimlane shows 'NetworkPolicy Egress Filter', bottom swimlane shows 'CoreDNS / NodeLocal Cache'. Step 1 (Small Query): Pod sends UDP query (<512 bytes) for 'alpaca-prod'; egress filter allows UDP/53; CoreDNS returns single IP answer; lookup succeeds. Step 2 (Large Query): Pod queries headless Service 'trainer.ml.svc.cluster.local' backing 30+ pods. UDP request reaches CoreDNS. Step 3 (Truncation): Response size exceeds 512 bytes / EDNS0 MTU. CoreDNS sets TC=1 (Truncation bit) in the DNS header and returns an empty answer section. Step 4 (Resolver Fallback): Pod resolver detects TC=1 and immediately initiates a TCP handshake (SYN) to port 53. Step 5 splits into two outcomes. Path A (Misconfigured Policy allowing only UDP/53): NetworkPolicy drops TCP SYN; client resolver hangs silently until default 5s timeout, returning SERVFAIL or EAI_AGAIN. Path B (Correct Policy allowing UDP/53 and TCP/53): TCP SYN passes; 3-way handshake completes; full multi-IP answer is delivered over TCP stream successfully.
alt: A sequence flow shows a large DNS response setting the UDP truncation bit and failing when an egress network policy allows UDP 53 but blocks TCP 53.
cap: When large DNS responses set the truncation bit, resolvers fall back to TCP port 53, which fails unless egress NetworkPolicies explicitly permit both UDP and TCP.

name: p4-0515-tofqdns-proxy
title: Cilium toFQDNs DNS proxy and dynamic eBPF map population
spec: Sequence and packet flow diagram across three vertical swimlanes: Left Lane (Trainer Pod: app=trainer in namespace training), Middle Lane (Cilium Node Agent: tc BPF hook, Per-node DNS Proxy on port 53, and cilium_policy_<ep_id> BPF map), Right Lane (Upstream: kube-dns in kube-system and Hugging Face CDN IP 108.156.60.42:443). Step 1: Trainer pod sends DNS request for *.huggingface.co over UDP 53. Step 2: Kernel tc BPF hook intercepts UDP 53 query due to rules.dns matchPattern: '*' and redirects it to the local Cilium DNS Proxy. Step 3: DNS proxy forwards request to kube-dns, receives response IP 108.156.60.42 with TTL 300s, and relays response back to Trainer pod. Step 4: DNS proxy extracts IP 108.156.60.42 matching *.huggingface.co and writes dynamic entry (IP=108.156.60.42, Port=443, Proto=TCP, Action=ALLOW, TTL=300s) directly into cilium_policy_<ep_id> BPF map. Step 5: Trainer pod sends TCP SYN to 108.156.60.42:443; kernel eBPF egress hook performs O(1) lookup in cilium_policy_<ep_id>, finds ALLOW, and transmits packet to wire without user-space proxy latency.
alt: A five-step packet flow showing how Cilium DNS proxy inspects DNS replies to dynamically populate resolved IP addresses into the eBPF policy map for FQDN egress.
