cap: Cilium toFQDNs rules rely on the DNS rule to redirect queries to a local DNS proxy, which inspects answers and injects ephemeral IP addresses with TTLs into the kernel eBPF policy map.

name: p4-0515-identity-models
title: Workload identity enforcement: Calico Dikastes sidecar versus Cilium kernel eBPF
anchor: ### Network identity with Calico and Cilium
spec: Side-by-side architectural comparison diagram. Left Box (Calico + Dikastes Sidecar Model): Pod contains Application Container (app: summary), Envoy Sidecar Container, and Dikastes Sidecar Container. Incoming packet with Istio mTLS client certificate arrives at Envoy; Envoy verifies certificate against Istio CA, then issues gRPC CheckRequest over local Unix Domain Socket (/var/run/dikastes/dikastes.sock) to Dikastes. Felix agent on host resolves Kubernetes ServiceAccount 'customer' to Pod IPs and programs Dikastes; Dikastes evaluates GlobalNetworkPolicy and returns Allow/Deny to Envoy. Right Box (Cilium Datapath eBPF Model): Application Pod runs with ServiceAccount 'leia'. Cilium control plane assigns numeric Security Identity (e.g. Identity 1597 for 'luke', 57962 for divergent pod). Inbound packet carries Security Identity 1597 in encapsulation/metadata. At the kernel tc BPF hook on the veth pair, BPF program performs O(1) lookup in BPF map cilium_policy_<ep_id> keyed by numeric source identity, destination port, and protocol, enforcing decision in kernel space without sidecar containers or Unix domain socket hops.
alt: A side-by-side architectural comparison of Calico Dikastes sidecar proxy model versus Cilium kernel eBPF numeric security identity model for workload authorization.
cap: Calico pairs an Envoy sidecar and Dikastes daemon communicating over Unix sockets for service-account identity, whereas Cilium embeds numeric security identities directly into datapath eBPF maps.

name: p4-0516-kms-envelope
title: KMS v2 Envelope Encryption in kube-apiserver
spec: Flow diagram showing write and read paths through kube-apiserver envelope encryption. Left box: 'API Client' submits Secret YAML with plaintext base64 payload. Center box: 'kube-apiserver' containing: (1) 'DEK Generator' producing an ephemeral Data Encryption Key, (2) 'Local Cipher' encrypting the Secret data with DEK, (3) 'gRPC KMS Client' communicating over a Unix domain socket with an external KMS plugin. Right box: 'External KMS Provider' (Cloud KMS / Vault Transit) holding Key Encryption Key (KEK). Step 1: Client sends POST/PUT Secret. Step 2: API server generates fresh DEK. Step 3: API server sends DEK to KMS plugin over gRPC. Step 4: KMS encrypts DEK with KEK and returns ciphertext DEK. Step 5: API server encrypts Secret payload with plaintext DEK, then discards plaintext DEK from memory. Step 6: API server writes combined record to etcd with prefix 'k8s:enc:kms:v2:<provider-name>:' containing encrypted DEK and ciphertext Secret payload. Bottom box: 'etcd storage' showing key '/registry/secrets/ns/name' storing only ciphertext.
alt: A diagram shows kube-apiserver using an external KMS provider to encrypt a data encryption key and storing the resulting ciphertext payload in etcd.
cap: KMS v2 envelope encryption uses an external Key Encryption Key to wrap a local Data Encryption Key, ensuring etcd stores only ciphertext.

name: p4-0516-secrets-store-csi
title: Secrets Store CSI Driver Architecture and Lifecycle
anchor: ### Secrets Store CSI driver and CyberArk
spec: Component interaction diagram spanning three zones: Cluster/Pod, Node Host, and External Secret Store. In Cluster/Pod zone: A Pod spec references volume 'secrets-api' with driver 'secrets-store.csi.k8s.com' and volumeAttributes 'secretProviderClass: apitoken'. In Node Host zone: 'Kubelet Volume Manager' triggers mount; talks over local gRPC socket to 'secrets-store-csi-driver DaemonSet Pod'; CSI driver invokes host provider binary '/etc/kubernetes/secrets-store-csi-providers/vault/provider-vault'. In External Secret Store zone: 'HashiCorp Vault / Cloud Secret Manager' receives authenticated request from provider using the Pod ServiceAccount token. Arrows: (1) Kubelet calls CSI driver on container start. (2) CSI driver executes provider-vault with parameters from SecretProviderClass. (3) Provider fetches secret '/secret/team-a' key 'apitoken' from Vault. (4) Provider writes payload to tmpfs mount at '/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/secrets-store-inline/mount'. (5) Container consumes mounted file at '/etc/secrets/apitoken'. Callout box explicitly highlights: 'Zero persistence in etcd: native Kubernetes Secret is never created'.
alt: A diagram illustrates the Secrets Store CSI driver fetching secrets directly from an external store into a node tmpfs mount without storing them in etcd.
cap: The Secrets Store CSI Driver mounts external secrets directly into pod tmpfs via a node provider plugin, completely bypassing etcd storage.

name: p4-0516-workload-identity
title: Keyless Workload Identity Federation Flow
spec: Sequence flow across four vertical swimlanes: 'Training Pod', 'kube-apiserver (OIDC Issuer)', 'Cloud STS / IAM (AWS/GCP/Azure)', and 'Cloud Storage (S3/GCS Checkpoints Bucket)'. Step 1 (Pod -> kube-apiserver): Pod requests or mounts projected ServiceAccount token with audience 'sts.googleapis.com' or 'sts.amazonaws.com' via TokenRequest API. Step 2 (Pod -> Cloud STS): Pod presents short-lived PSAT JWT to Cloud STS endpoint requesting temporary cloud credentials. Step 3 (Cloud STS -> kube-apiserver): Cloud STS contacts cluster public OIDC discovery endpoint '/.well-known/openid-configuration' and fetches signing keys from 'jwks_uri' to cryptographically verify the JWT signature. Step 4 (Cloud STS -> Pod): Cloud STS evaluates IAM trust policy matching 'sub: system:serviceaccount:team-a:trainer' and returns short-lived federated Cloud IAM OAuth/STS token (e.g., valid for 1 hour). Step 5 (Pod -> Cloud Storage): Training job directly reads training datasets and writes model checkpoint blobs to bucket using the temporary IAM token. Bottom banner notes: 'Zero static cloud API keys or passwords stored in Kubernetes Secrets or Git'.
alt: A sequence diagram shows a pod exchanging its projected ServiceAccount token with a cloud STS service via cluster OIDC keys to obtain short-lived cloud credentials.
cap: Workload Identity Federation verifies Kubernetes projected tokens against the cluster OIDC endpoint to issue short-lived cloud credentials without static keys.

name: p4-0518-volcano-architecture
title: Volcano batch scheduling action pipeline and plugin interaction
spec: A three-tier horizontal architectural diagram. Top tier: Custom resources including vcjob / PodGroup with minMember: 4 and minResources: {nvidia.com/gpu: 32}, pointing to a Volcano Queue with configured weight, capability, and reclaimable settings. Middle tier: The Volcano Scheduler executing its five-stage cyclic action pipeline: 1. enqueue (admits queued jobs based on queue capability), 2. allocate (evaluates candidate nodes for gang allocation), 3. preempt (evicts lower-priority pods within the same queue), 4. reclaim (reclaims quota across queues according to dominant resource fairness weights), and 5. backfill (places small tasks onto idle GPU slots). Bottom tier: Plugin layer invoked during actions, showing gang (checks minMember threshold before assigning), drf (calculates dominant resource shares), binpack (maximizes node utilization), and task-topology / numa-aware (optimizes network hops and socket placement). Arrows show pods directly bound to target nodes via schedulerName: volcano.
alt: Volcano batch scheduling pipeline showing enqueue, allocate, preempt, reclaim, and backfill actions coordinating with gang and fairness plugins.
cap: Volcano replaces kube-scheduler for batch workloads, evaluating all-or-nothing PodGroup admission and cross-queue fairness in a multi-stage action loop.

name: p4-0518-placement-lifecycle
title: Placement lifecycle: kube-scheduler, descheduler, and autoscaler coordination
spec: A closed-loop coordination diagram showing three independent controllers operating on cluster node capacity and pod lifecycle. 1. kube-scheduler: Reads pending pods from activeQ, evaluates feasible nodes via Filter and Score (configured with percentageOfNodesToScore: 50 and parallelism: 16), and packs pods using MostAllocated scoring; unschedulable pods remain Pending. 2. Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter: Observes Pending pods, provisions new GPU nodes (or triggers atomic ProvisioningRequests), and cordons/terminates idle nodes after cool-down. 3. Descheduler: Periodically scans running workloads, applying strategies like LowNodeUtilization to consolidate fragmented GPU nodes and RemovePodsViolatingTopologySpreadConstraint; respects PodDisruptionBudgets (PDB) while strictly ignoring training pods marked with descheduler.alpha.kubernetes.io/evict: 'false'. Evicted pods re-enter the scheduling queue for defragmented placement.
alt: Three control loops coordinate placement: kube-scheduler places pods, the descheduler periodically evicts drifted pods to consolidate nodes, and the autoscaler provisions or removes nodes.
cap: Maintaining optimal GPU cluster placement requires coordinating kube-scheduler placement, descheduler defragmentation, and autoscaler provisioning without interrupting running training jobs.

name: p4-0525-gpu-hw-ladder
title: GPU and Fabric Hardware Diagnostic Ladder
spec: A vertical 5-tier diagnostic ladder showing the order of inspection for GPU and fabric hardware failures on worker nodes. Tier 1 (top): 'High-Level Driver & Health' with commands 'nvidia-smi --query-gpu=... --format=csv' and 'dcgmi health -c; dcgmi diag -r 2', checking active throttling reasons, temperatures, power cap, and ECC uncorrected errors. Tier 2: 'NVLink & Fabric Topology' with commands 'nvidia-smi topo -m', 'nvidia-smi nvlink -s', and 'systemctl status nvidia-fabricmanager', checking link states and NVLink errors. Tier 3: 'PCIe Bus & Link Negotiation' with command 'lspci -vv -s <addr> | grep -E "LnkSta|LnkCap|AER"', showing a comparison box: 'LnkCap (Rated Gen5 x16)' vs 'LnkSta (Negotiated: e.g. Gen3 x4 downgraded)' and AER error counters. Tier 4: 'Kernel & Driver Hardware Events' with commands 'dmesg -T | grep -i xid' and 'journalctl -k | grep -E "Xid|NVRM"', listing common hardware fault codes 'Xid 13, 31, 43, 61, 74, 79 (Fallen off bus)'. Tier 5: 'Inter-Node Fabric & Collectives' with commands 'ibstat; rdma link', 'all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 1G -f 2 -g 8', and 'NCCL_DEBUG=INFO'. A side callout at the bottom points to 'Evidence Snapshot' before any cordon or reboot: 'sudo nvidia-bug-report.sh -> nvidia-bug-report.log.gz'.
alt: A five-tier diagnostic ladder for GPU and fabric hardware inspecting driver health, NVLink, PCIe link status, kernel Xid errors, and collective fabric tests before collecting a bug report.
cap: GPU and fabric hardware triage moves through five layers from NVML queries down to PCIe link negotiation and kernel Xid errors before generating an official bug report.

name: p4-0601-custom-vs-commodity
title: Architectural Spectrum: Custom Supercomputer, Commodity HPC Cluster, Beowulf Cluster, and Computing Farm
anchor: ### Clusters versus custom vendor supercomputers, farms, and Beowulf systems
spec: Four parallel comparison columns arranged horizontally to contrast the four system paradigms discussed in the section text: 1. 'Custom Supercomputer': Examples 'IBM Blue Gene series', 'NEC SX-Aurora Tsubasa'; Hardware: Proprietary compute boards, custom chassis, single-vendor backplanes, proprietary specialized interconnects (e.g., 3D torus); Sourcing & Spares: Single-vendor lock-in, parts cannot be bought separately on open market, vendor roadmap dependency; Tooling: Vendor-specific proprietary utilities and custom diagnostics; Coupling: Microsecond tightly coupled. 2. 'Commodity HPC / AI Cluster': Examples 'Modern TOP500 & GPU AI Training Clusters'; Hardware: Commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) standard enterprise servers, x86/ARM/GPU accelerator modules (PCIe/OAM); Sourcing & Spares: Multi-vendor sourcing, standardized components, replaceable parts; Interconnect: Off-the-shelf low-latency fabrics (InfiniBand, RoCEv2, Slingshot); Tooling: Open tools, Linux, Slurm, MPI, NCCL, parallel shell scripts; Coupling: Microsecond tightly coupled. 3. 'Beowulf Cluster': Examples 'Improvised academic or DIY clusters'; Hardware: Assembled from commodity consumer/office PCs; Sourcing & Spares: Budget parts, consumer retail channels; Interconnect: Standard commodity Ethernet LAN (1G/10G) switches without specialized RDMA; Tooling: Linux and open-source clustering tools; Coupling: Loosely to moderately coupled. 4. 'Computing Farm': Examples 'Render farms', 'Parameter sweep workers', 'SETI@home / Folding@home'; Hardware: Heterogeneous servers or cloud VMs running independently; Sourcing & Spares: Completely flexible, no matching hardware required; Interconnect: Standard TCP/IP LAN or WAN; Tooling: Central batch dispatcher, independent task pull; Coupling: Decoupled (zero inter-node communication). A bottom highlight box summarizes: Modern AI supercomputers are almost universally Commodity Clusters with high-speed RDMA fabrics and synchronization hardware, offering multi-vendor freedom and open tooling while achieving top capability.
alt: Comparison of custom supercomputers, commodity HPC clusters, Beowulf systems, and computing farms across components, interconnect, vendor lock-in, and target workloads.
cap: Modern supercomputing centers predominantly deploy commodity off-the-shelf clusters with standardized fabrics rather than proprietary single-vendor supercomputers or improvised Beowulf systems.

name: p4-0607-install-methods
title: Four Slurm installation methods and silent build-time dependency drops
spec: Top half: A 4-column comparison matrix comparing the four installation approaches. Column 1: 'Distro Packages (apt / dnf EPEL)' with roles (Controller: slurm-slurmctld, slurm-plugins; Compute: slurm-slurmd; DB: slurm-slurmdbd, slurm-sql, mariadb; Login: slurm-sackd), pros (fast, zero compile), cons (outdated version, inflexible build flags). Column 2: 'Source Builds (rpmbuild / debuild / tarball)' with configure flags (--prefix=/opt/slurm), custom RPM/DEB packaging, pros (exact version, reproducible image), cons (requires build toolchain). Column 3: 'Cluster Managers (BCM, DGX OS)' with turnkey image, automated config, pros (supported stack), cons (black-box defaults). Column 4: 'Containerized (Slinky, Soperator)' with K8s Pods/DaemonSets, GitOps deployment, pros (cloud-native lifecycle), cons (layering complexity). Bottom half: Callout box on the 'Silent Compile-Time Drop Pitfall'. Flow diagram showing ./configure running on build host: checks for nvml.h -> IF MISSING: builds without AutoDetect=nvml (GPU autodetection broken at runtime without error); checks for mysql_config -> IF MISSING: omits slurmdbd MySQL support; checks for dbus -> IF MISSING: omits cgroup v2 plugin support. Emphasizes installing development headers BEFORE building.
alt: Comparison of four Slurm installation methods alongside the silent compile-time feature drop hazard when development headers are missing.
cap: Choose source RPM or DEB packages for production GPU clusters, and install nvml, mysql, and dbus headers before compilation to avoid silent feature drops.

name: p4-0607-rpc-overload-cascade
title: The controller RPC overload cascade, lock contention, and diagnosis with sdiag
anchor: ### 7. "Socket timed out on send/recv operation" and a sluggish controller: RPC overload
spec: Left panel: The Polling Storm (Root Causes). Box showing three abusive request sources: 1) User terminal polling scripts (while true; do squeue; sleep 1; done), 2) External monitoring exporters querying squeue every 5s across hundreds of clients, 3) High-churn short jobs flooding job state changes. All send RPCs (port 6817) into slurmctld. Center panel: The slurmctld Contention Cascade. Incoming RPC queue exceeds thread pool limit -> Threads acquire global in-memory job read lock (job_read_lock) -> Read locks starve write locks (scheduling, node state updates, slurmd heartbeats) -> Backfill scheduler cycle time spikes from 0.05s to 15s+ -> slurmd ping heartbeats queue behind read requests -> Controller marks healthy nodes DOWN* (flapping). Right panel: Symptoms and Diagnosis with sdiag. Top error bubble: Client squeue hangs with 'Socket timed out on send/recv operation'. Diagnosis terminal showing sdiag output: 'Remote Procedure Call statistics by message type' highlighting REQUEST_JOB_INFO (92% of calls), 'RPCs by user' identifying abusive user UID, Agent queue size saturated. Bottom panel: Operational Remedies: 1) Throttle and cache polling; 2) Replace squeue polling with sacct or caching exporters; 3) Configure RPC rate limiting; 4) Raise MaxJobCount only after eliminating pollers.
alt: Diagram of an RPC overload cascade in slurmctld showing how tight polling loops monopolize global read locks, delay scheduling, and appear in sdiag output.
cap: A polling storm holds internal controller locks and delays scheduling, producing connection timeouts that can be isolated using sdiag RPC statistics.

name: p4-0610-live-monitoring
title: Live GPU Job Telemetry and Distributed Bottleneck Triage
anchor: ### Live GPU job monitoring and distributed profiling (*Distributed AI Systems* Chapter 8)
spec: Flowchart and decision tree diagram organized from top to bottom. Top tier shows two non-SSH telemetry collection methods: Box A labeled 'SLURM Step Attachment' with command 'srun --jobid=ID -w node nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used,memory.total --format=csv,noheader,nounits', and Box B labeled 'Interactive Job Inspection' with 'srun --jobid=ID nvidia-smi'. Middle tier splits into three diagnostic symptom branches based on query values: Left branch labeled 'Condition: utilization.gpu < 50%' leads to 'Straggler / Stalled Rank' box, with callout causes: DataLoader starvation (insufficient cpus-per-task), slow storage I/O, or collective barrier wait. Center branch labeled 'Condition: memory_used / memory_total > 0.95' leads to 'Imminent VRAM OOM' box, with callouts: CUDA caching allocator fragmentation or activation memory spike within 5% of HBM exhaustion. Right branch labeled 'Condition: utilization.gpu == 100% but slow step time' leads to 'False 100% Compute Illusion' box. An arrow from Right branch points to Bottom tier profiling action: 'torch.profiler Instrumentation (5 steps)' with calls 'prof.key_averages().table(sort_by=cuda_time_total)' and rank-0 Chrome trace 'prof.export_chrome_trace(trace.json)'. Profiler diagnosis outcome box shows: 'ncclAllReduce dominates cuda_time_total -> Inter-Node Communication Bottleneck (NCCL polling loops spinning SMs at 100%)', leading to remediation tags: 'Increase micro-batch size', 'Gradient accumulation', 'Overlap comm/compute', 'export NCCL_DEBUG=INFO'.
alt: A troubleshooting flowchart showing how live GPU metrics and torch.profiler distinguish stragglers, impending memory exhaustion, and false 100 percent utilization caused by NCCL polling loops.
cap: Live GPU telemetry reveals true bottlenecks by distinguishing idle stragglers, VRAM exhaustion, and false 100 percent utilization from NCCL spin loops.

name: p4-0611-job-lifecycle
title: The 6-Stage Slurm Job Life Cycle
anchor: ### The 6-stage Slurm job life cycle (*Supercomputers for Linux Sysadmins* Chapter 15)
spec: Horizontal sequence diagram showing the 6 stages of a Slurm job with actors, daemons, and failure branches. Stage 1: Submission. Initiator sbatch/srun/salloc sends request to slurmctld (controller); checks association and QoS limits; invokes SPANK plugins (e.g., pyxis --container-image) and job_submit plugins to validate or rewrite request before resources are allocated. Stage 2: Prolog. slurmctld dispatches to allocated nodes; slurmd executes root Prolog on every node; cleans /tmp, /dev/shm, and clears stale IPC semaphores; error branch: if Prolog exit != 0, Slurm aborts job launch, marks offending node as DRAIN, and requeues or cancels job. Stage 3: Step Creation. slurmd spawns slurmstepd; invokes step plugins; sets up task/cgroup for CPU, RAM, and GPU device constraints; starts Step 0 (batch script) on Node 0. Stage 4: Running. Batch script executes srun commands creating numbered steps (JOBID.0, JOBID.1); parallel background loop: slurmd periodically runs HealthCheckProgram at HealthCheckInterval to monitor dmesg and GPU health, draining failing nodes. Stage 5: Preemption (conditional). Higher-priority job triggers PreemptMode: REQUEUE, CANCEL, or SUSPEND,GANG. Stage 6: Termination. Job exits, gets cancelled, or hits --time limit; Slurm broadcasts SIGTERM to all allocated processes; KillWait timer counts down; Slurm follows with SIGKILL; slurmd runs root Epilog on every node to verify cleanup and free resources.
alt: A 6-stage flow diagram tracing a Slurm job from submission through root prolog, cgroup step creation, running with health checks, preemption modes, and termination cleanup.
cap: The 6-stage Slurm job life cycle moves from controller validation through root node preparation, cgroup containment, step execution, and cleanup.

name: p4-0611-job-array-architecture
title: Job Array Execution, Throttling, and Task Dispatch
spec: Architectural diagram illustrating how sbatch --array=0-99%10 script.sh executes. Top section: ID hierarchy and variables. Show Array Master Job ID SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID (variable %A, e.g., 12345), total count SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT (100 tasks), and task indices SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (%a, 0 through 99). Each task receives its own unique SLURM_JOB_ID (%j). Middle section: Throttling window. A sliding execution window of size %10 shows tasks 0 through 9 in state R (RUNNING) across compute nodes, while tasks 10 through 99 wait in state PD (PENDING). An arrow indicates that as task 0 completes, task 10 moves into the active execution window, protecting shared storage and scheduler fair-share. Bottom-left box: Config file indexing. Shows configs.txt with 1-based lines; command CONFIG=$(sed -n '$((SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID+1))p' configs.txt) maps task 0 to line 1, task 1 to line 2, avoiding off-by-one errors. Bottom-right box: Output logging and scancel control. Default output slurm-%A_%a.out produces individual logs slurm-12345_0.out, slurm-12345_1.out; callout contrasts scancel 12345 (cancels all 100 tasks) versus scancel 12345_7 (cancels only task index 7).
alt: A diagram of a Slurm job array showing how the master job ID and task IDs relate, how the percent throttle caps concurrent running tasks, and how configs and logs are mapped.
cap: A job array manages many identical requests under one master job ID, using a throttle window to protect storage and sed indexing to dispatch configurations.

name: p4-0612-hgx-rail-binding
title: Rail-Optimized HGX NUMA, GPU, and NIC Binding Architecture

name: p4-2004-proc-fd-triage
title: Triage Pipeline for Leaked File Descriptors via /proc and lsof
anchor: ### 3. Read /proc and lsof before you attach a tracer
spec: Flow diagram of descriptor triage on PID $pid. Step 1: inspect limits via grep 'Max open files' /proc/$pid/limits yielding soft limit (e.g. 1024) and hard limit (1048576). Step 2: count current descriptors with ls /proc/$pid/fd | wc -l. Step 3: aggregation pipeline ls -l /proc/$pid/fd | awk 'NR > 1 {print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head. Step 4 splits into four diagnostic target boxes: Box A (Regular file path repeated hundreds of times, e.g. /var/log/app.log) pointing to 'Bug: Missing close() call in file handler'. alt: Diagnostic pipeline grouping /proc/PID/fd symlink targets into regular file leaks, socket leaks, unlinked open files, and epoll instances.

name: p4-2004-noexec-bypass-mech
title: Kernel noexec Mount Enforcement versus Interpreter Execution
anchor: ### Scenario 4: mode 755 and still Permission denied
spec: Split diagram showing how a noexec mount affects direct binary execution versus interpreter execution. Context header shows mount at /mnt/data with flags 'rw,noexec,relatime' containing script run.sh with permissions 0755 (-rwxr-xr-x) owned by user u. Left panel: Direct execution './run.sh'. Step 1: Shell invokes execve('./run.sh', ...). Step 2: Linux VFS examines mount flags for /mnt/data and encounters MS_NOEXEC. Step 3: Kernel immediately halts execution and returns -1 EACCES. Step 4: Shell outputs 'Permission denied' with exit status 126; inode execute bits are never evaluated. Right panel: Interpreter execution 'sh run.sh'. Step 1: Shell invokes execve('/bin/sh', ['sh', 'run.sh']). Step 2: /bin/sh binary is on rootfs mounted with exec; execve succeeds. Step 3: Running sh process issues openat(AT_FDCWD, 'run.sh', O_RDONLY). Step 4: VFS checks read permission on run.sh; read is allowed by both mount flags ('rw') and inode mode ('r-x'). Step 5: Shell reads script text as data into memory and runs commands; prints 'it ran'. Bottom annotation notes remount fix: 'mount -o remount,bind,exec /mnt/data'.
alt: Diagram contrasting direct execution failing on a noexec mount via execve with interpreter execution succeeding via openat read.
cap: A noexec mount causes the kernel to fail execve with EACCES before inspecting file mode bits, whereas executing an interpreter reads the script file as plain data.

name: p4-2007-bash-pitfalls
title: Production Bash Pitfalls: pipefail, Local Masking, and Arithmetic Status
spec: Three horizontal comparison panels detailing silent failure traps in bash scripts. Panel 1 (Pipeline failure): Show pipeline 'false | true'. Without pipefail: 'false' exits 1, 'true' exits 0, resulting in overall status $? = 0 (silent failure masked). With 'set -o pipefail': pipe captures rightmost non-zero exit, resulting in $? = 1 (script halts or handles failure). Add note showing 'yes | head -1' closing pipe early, raising SIGPIPE (exit status 141) under pipefail, contrasted with 'awk NR<=5' reading without early pipe closure. Panel 2 (Local variable masking): Under 'set -e', show line 'local x=$(false)'. The subshell fails with status 1, but 'local' command itself succeeds with exit 0, causing set -e to ignore the failure. Show the fix: separate 'local x' followed by 'x=$(false)'. Panel 3 (Arithmetic exit code): Show 'set -e; i=0; ((i++))'. In bash 5.2, post-increment evaluates the expression to the old value 0, returning exit status 1 and terminating the script immediately. Show safe alternative 'i=$((i+1))' which always returns exit status 0.
alt: Three bash production pitfalls showing how unquoted pipes hide failures, local masks subshell exit codes, and arithmetic post-increment trips set -e.
cap: Shell safety flags like set -e require defensive coding because pipes, local assignments, and arithmetic expansions can silently mask or trigger exit codes.

name: p4-2007-auth-log-shift
title: Field Position Shifts in auth.log Between Valid and Invalid Users
spec: Side-by-side comparison illustrating why counting columns breaks on variable syslog lines. Top box: Valid user log line broken into numbered tokens: [1: Mar] [2: 12] [3: 10:14:02] [4: srv] [5: sshd[1234]:] [6: Failed] [7: password] [8: for] [9: root] [10: from] [11: 198.51.100.23] [12: port] [13: 45120] [14: ssh2]. Middle box: Invalid user log line broken into numbered tokens: [1: Mar] [2: 12] [3: 10:14:05] [4: srv] [5: sshd[1235]:] [6: Failed] [7: password] [8: for] [9: invalid] [10: user] [11: admin] [12: from] [13: 198.51.100.23] [14: port] [15: 45122] [16: ssh2]. alt: Comparison of auth.log lines showing how invalid user insertions shift column 11 from an IP address to a username.
cap: Log lines with variable phrase counts shift positional fields, making delimiter-anchored regular expressions far more reliable than fixed column extraction.

name: p4-2008-go-python-bridge
title: Python standard library tools and their Go equivalents
spec: A side-by-side comparison matrix with 4 columns: Feature / Pattern, Python stdlib tool, Go equivalent implementation, and Interview trade-off note. Row 1: 'Frequency counting' -> Python: 'Counter(s)' -> Go: 'map[rune]int' with 'm[r]++' -> Note: Go maps return the zero value (0) on missing keys, eliminating the need for defaultdict. Row 2: 'Priority Queue / Heap' -> Python: 'heapq.heappush / heappop' (built-in min-heap over list) -> Go: 'container/heap' requiring custom slice type 'intHeap []int' implementing 5 interface methods: 'Len()', 'Less()', 'Swap()', 'Push(any)', 'Pop() any' with pointer receivers -> Note: High interview boilerplate in Go; know the 5 methods by heart or use Python. Row 3: 'Binary search lower bound' -> Python: 'bisect.bisect_left(a, x)' -> Go: 'sort.SearchInts(a, x)' -> Note: Both return the first index where element >= x. Row 4: 'Sorting stability' -> Python: 'list.sort()' (Timsort, guaranteed stable) -> Go: 'sort.Slice()' (unstable) vs 'sort.SliceStable()' (stable) -> Note: Go requires explicit SliceStable to preserve order of equal keys. Row 5: 'String element access' -> Python: 'for ch in s' (characters) -> Go: 'for _, r := range s' (yields runes, not raw bytes) -> Note: Slicing bytes directly in Go can corrupt multi-byte UTF-8 characters.
alt: A comparison diagram detailing Python standard library tools alongside their Go equivalents and boilerplate requirements for coding interviews.

name: p4-2009-blast-radius-bfs

name: p4-2009-union-find
title: Union-Find with Union by Size and Path Compression
spec: Three-stage visual state diagram of disjoint set trees representing failing node clusters. Left panel (Initial Clusters): Two trees of failing rack nodes. Tree A with root Node A (size 3) with children Node B and Node C. Tree D with root Node D (size 2) with child Node E, and Node E has child Node F. Middle panel (Union by Size): An edge links Node B and Node E. Find identifies root A (size 3) and root D (size 2). Because size(D) < size(A), root D is attached under root A, pointing D -> A, updating size(A) to 5. Right panel (Path Compression during Find): A call to find(F) traverses F -> E -> D -> A. Path compression executes iteratively, updating parent pointers so Node E and Node F both point directly to root Node A, reducing tree height to 1 and enabling constant-time subsequent lookups.
alt: Union by size attaches smaller root trees under larger ones, while path compression flattens deep parent pointers directly to the root during find operations.
cap: Union by size keeps disjoint trees shallow by attaching smaller clusters under larger roots, while path compression flattens parent chains directly to the root on each lookup.

name: p4-2010-insert-vs-deque
title: Memory Mechanics of list.insert versus deque.appendleft
anchor: ### 2. The hidden costs of Python operations, measured
spec: Two-panel vertical diagram contrasting memory operations during head insertions. Top panel: list.insert(0, x). Shows a contiguous array in memory holding references [item 0, item 1, item 2, ... item n-1]. An incoming element 'x' targets index 0. Big red directional arrows show every single item from index 0 to n-1 shifting one position to the right ('Shifts every item in contiguous memory'). Annotations show measured timings: '1,000 items: 0.61 us' and '100,000 items: 30 us (O(n) linear growth)'. Bottom panel: deque.appendleft(x). Shows collections.deque implemented as doubly linked blocks of pointers. The leftmost block has an available empty slot at the head. The incoming element 'x' is placed directly into the free slot without moving any existing elements ('Writes to free slot in head block'). Annotations show measured timings: '1,000 items: 0.014 us' and '100,000 items: 0.16 us (O(1) flat, within noise)'. Summary text box at bottom: 'At 100,000 items, list head insertion is ~187x slower because shifting contiguous memory scales with n, whereas deque prepends in constant time.'
alt: Comparison of list.insert shifting every contiguous element to the right versus deque.appendleft placing an element into a free head slot without shifting.
cap: Inserting at the head of a list requires shifting every reference in contiguous memory taking 30 microseconds at 100,000 items, while deque.appendleft takes 0.16 microseconds in constant time.

name: p4-2013-retry-cascade
title: Worked Retry Storm Cascade Arithmetic and Defense Architecture
spec: Two-panel layout contrasting failure cascade arithmetic with the four-part defense architecture. Left panel titled 'Uncontrolled Retry Storm Cascade': show 10 total replicas serving 100% capacity; 2 replicas fail leaving 8 replicas (80% remaining capacity); 5% initial error rate triggers 3 unbudgeted client retries per failed request (5% * 3 = 15% added load); total offered load becomes 100% + 15% = 115%; effective load on 8 surviving replicas is 115% / 80% = 144% load saturation; downward arrow showing queue buildup, timeouts, further retries, and total collapse. Right panel titled 'The Four-Part Defense Architecture': box 1 'Pre-first-token only' (only requests failing before first token are eligible for retry; partial streams abort to avoid nondeterministic replays); box 2 '10% Retry Budget Cap' (gateway rejects retries exceeding 10% of total normal traffic); box 3 'Jittered Exponential Backoff' (retries disperse smoothly instead of synchronized waves); box 4 'Single-layer Retries with 429 Shedding' (retries execute only at gateway, never stacked with SDK; router sheds full queues immediately with HTTP 429 and Retry-After header).
alt: Comparison of retry storm load escalation arithmetic against the four-point defense architecture of retry budgets, jitter, pre-token guards, and 429 shedding.
cap: Losing two replicas while retrying three times amplifies load to 144 percent of capacity, which is prevented by a 10 percent retry budget, pre-token retries, and 429 shedding.

spec:

Left-to-right flow: An incoming Customer Request reaches a high-level box 'Gateway Layer (Edge SLI Measurement)', passes to 'Router', then to 'Engine Layer (vLLM Execution)', which drives 'Hardware & Platform Layers (GPU, Node, K8s)'.

name: p4-2020-multimodel-placement
title: Multi-Model Placement Strategies and Disaggregated Autoscaling
spec: Two-part diagram comparing multi-model topology options and disaggregated scaling axes. Top half: Placement comparison. Left side shows Latency-Optimised Dedicated Fleet: Client Traffic reaches a Model Router; Router dispatches Model A requests to 'Dedicated Model A Pool' (Floor=3, always-on GPUs, preserved prefix cache), and Model B requests to 'Dedicated Model B Pool' (Floor=0 or 1, quiet model, scaled independently). Right side shows Cost-Optimised Shared Fleet: Router dispatches to 'Shared GPU Pool' where instances dynamically load/evict weights on demand from shared storage, labeled with 'Cold Start Penalty: 10s-60s delay' and 'Cache Thrashing'. Bottom half: Disaggregated Fleet and Cache-Aware Scaling. Shows incoming traffic split by request phase: Prefill Workers (scale on prompt tokens / arrival burst) feed KV tensors over high-speed network to Decode Workers (scale on active concurrent sequences and output token length). An alert box highlights 'Scale-in Warning / Miss Storm': when a replica is terminated, its warm local prefix cache is discarded, causing downstream requests to suffer full prefill latency.
alt: A diagram contrasting dedicated always-on pools against shared on-demand pools, alongside disaggregated prefill and decode worker autoscaling with prefix cache eviction risks.
cap: Dedicated pools isolate hot model scaling and protect prefix caches, while disaggregated serving enables prefill and decode pools to scale on their distinct bottlenecks.

name: p4-2021-deploy-grace-period
title: Grace Period Sizing to Prevent Rolling Update Stream Truncation
anchor: ### Scenario C. Streams die on every deploy
spec: A comparative timeline diagram contrasting the default Kubernetes termination timeline with the production-sized 135-second grace period for LLM inference pods. Top Timeline (Default 30s Grace Period): At t=0s, deployment rolls replica. Pod holds ~40 active streams lasting up to 90s. SIGTERM sent; endpoint removal races in parallel. At t=30s, termination grace period expires. Kubelet sends SIGKILL. Callout: 'SIGKILL at 30s truncates running 90s streams mid-generation. First token already delivered, so streams cannot be retried!'. Bottom Timeline (Production Grace Period = 135s): Structured in sequential blocks matching the worked arithmetic: Block 1 (t=0s to 5s): 'preStop sleep (5s) allows router EndpointSlice propagation across all proxies; router marks replica as draining'. Block 2 (t=5s to 125s): 'SIGTERM received by engine (--shutdown-timeout > 0). Max allowed stream duration (120s stream cap) allows active streams to finish generating'. Block 3 (t=125s to 135s): '10s safety margin buffer before SIGKILL'. Bottom summary formula: 'Grace Period = 5s (preStop sleep) + 120s (longest allowed stream) + 10s (margin) = 135s'. Side annotation: 'Roll 1 pod at a time; wait for readiness probe before proceeding to maintain spare capacity above X+1'.
alt: A timeline comparing the default 30-second Kubernetes grace period cutting 90-second streams with SIGKILL against a 135-second budget combining a 5-second preStop sleep, 120-second stream cap, and 10-second margin.
cap: Sizing the termination grace period to 135 seconds covers endpoint propagation and the maximum stream duration, preventing SIGKILL from truncating active generations.

name: p4-2022-engine-specialties
title: Serving Engine and Orchestrator Specialisations
spec: A comparative layout with 5 architectural cards arranged horizontally or in a clean 2-row grid. Card 1: 'vLLM (Engine + Server)'. Highlights: Paged KV caching, continuous batching, single model per instance, broad open-source community, rapid adoption of open checkpoints. Card 2: 'TensorRT-LLM (Engine + Server)'. Highlights: Dedicated NVIDIA optimisation, PyTorch LLM API with trtllm-serve, in-flight batching, disaggregated prefill/decode (Beta), chunked context, FP8/FP4 quantisation. Card 3: 'SGLang (Engine + Server)'. Highlights: RadixAttention (radix tree for prefix reuse), structured output, agentic workloads, broad hardware support. Card 4: 'Triton (Inference Server)'. Highlights: Model repository with configuration files, dynamic batcher, instance groups across multiple GPUs, hosts TensorRT-LLM or classic vision/tabular models under one API. Card 5: 'Ray Serve LLM (Fleet Orchestrator)'. Highlights: Ray head and worker nodes, prefix-aware routing to warm cache replicas, autoscaling, disaggregated prefill and decode workers hosting vLLM or SGLang engines underneath.
alt: A comparison of vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, Triton, and Ray Serve LLM showing their architectural mechanisms and workload targets.
cap: Figure 20.22.3. Each tool solves a different operational problem, from kernel-level NVIDIA tuning in TensorRT-LLM to fleet-level prefix routing in Ray Serve.

name: p4-2022-customer-engine-decision

spec: A decision flowchart illustrating how an SRE selects the serving stack. Start node: 'New Customer Serving Request'. Decision Diamond 1: 'Stable large model (e.g., 70B) on NVIDIA GPUs with strict TTFT SLO for 1+ year?' -> Yes: Box 'TensorRT-LLM on TP=8 (Benchmark against vLLM; efficiency gains justify tight hardware and version coupling)'. -> No: Decision Diamond 2: 'Fleet of 40+ diverse open models changing frequently across mixed hardware?' -> Yes: Box 'vLLM (One process per model, paged caching, fastest path to production)'. -> No: Decision Diamond 3: 'Mixed workloads including non-LLM models (vision, audio, tabular) needing one metrics and health API?' -> Yes: Box 'Triton Server (Model repository with dynamic batcher hosting LLM and non-LLM backends)'. -> No: Decision Diamond 4: 'Need cluster autoscaling and prefix-aware routing across many engine instances?' -> Yes: Box 'Ray Serve LLM orchestrating vLLM or SGLang'. name: p4-2023-drill1-scheduler-filter
title: Scheduler Node Filtering for a Pending GPU Pod
anchor: ### Drill 1: Pending pod that requests nvidia.com/gpu
spec: Top block: Incoming Pod 'llama-gpu' with spec 'limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1' and 'tolerations: []' (empty). Downward arrows point to kube-scheduler running Filter plugins across 6 cluster nodes split into two pools: Left column (Untainted CPU Nodes): 2 nodes with 'Allocatable nvidia.com/gpu: 0'. Scheduler evaluates 'NodeResourcesFit' plugin -> Fails with '2 Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu'. Right column (Tainted GPU Nodes): 4 nodes with 'Allocatable nvidia.com/gpu: 8' and Taint 'nvidia.com/gpu=true:NoSchedule'. Scheduler evaluates 'TaintToleration' plugin -> Fails with '4 node(s) had untolerated taint(s)'. Middle summary bubble: Scheduler produces aggregate event '0/6 nodes are available: 4 node(s) had untolerated taint(s), 2 Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' -> Pod status remains Pending. Bottom block: The Fix: Manifest patch adding toleration 'key: nvidia.com/gpu, operator: Exists, effect: NoSchedule'. An arrow shows the patched pod bypassing the TaintToleration filter, unlocking scheduling onto GPU node 1 (6 of 8 GPUs used, 2 free).
alt: Scheduler filtering divides six nodes into two untainted nodes rejected for insufficient GPUs and four GPU nodes rejected for untolerated taints, resolved by adding the matching toleration.
cap: A scheduler FailedScheduling event breaks down by node pool, showing how untolerated taints on GPU nodes and zero GPUs on CPU nodes leave no schedulable placement until a toleration is added.

name: p4-2025-group-left-join
title: Many-to-One Vector Matching with group_left
spec: Layout shows two columns joining into an output vector, illustrating why Prometheus requires explicit group_left. On the left side ('Many' side), show two series of metric vllm:num_requests_waiting: series 1 with labels pod='pod-1', engine='0', value 7; series 2 with labels pod='pod-1', engine='1', value 4. On the right side ('One' side), show kube_pod_info with labels pod='pod-1', node='node-a', value 1. In the middle, show the join attempt: Top branch shows bad query 'waiting * on (pod) kube_pod_info' marked with a red X and promtool error callout: 'multiple matches for labels: many-to-one matching must be explicit (group_left/group_right)'. Bottom branch shows the correct query 'waiting * on (pod) group_left(node) kube_pod_info' marked with a green checkmark. Show arrows matching on pod='pod-1' and copying node='node-a' to both output series: output 1 is pod='pod-1', engine='0', node='node-a', value 7; output 2 is pod='pod-1', engine='1', node='node-a', value 4.

name: p4-2025-cardinality-explosion
title: Cardinality Arithmetic and Label Explosion
anchor: ### 12. Cardinality: the cost behind every label
spec: A tree calculation layout illustrating label multiplication and TSDB memory cost. Level 1 (Histogram base): A single histogram metric with 10 finite buckets + 1 '+Inf' bucket + 1 '_sum' + 1 '_count' = 13 series per label set. Level 2 (Model dimension): Multiply by 20 models -> 13 * 20 = 260 series. Level 3 (Tenant dimension): Multiply by 1,000 tenants -> 260 * 1,000 = 260,000 active series in memory (healthy TSDB state). Level 4 (The Anti-Pattern): A red fork showing the addition of label 'request_id'. Unbounded unique request IDs per day (e.g. 5,000,000 requests) multiply by 260,000 -> billions of series leading to TSDB Out of Memory crash. At the bottom, contrast two destination boxes: 'Metrics TSDB' showing only bounded low-cardinality labels (model, status), versus 'Traces and Logs' showing unbounded high-cardinality data (request_id, prompt_id, user_id).
alt: A diagram showing series multiplication across ten histogram buckets, twenty models, and one thousand tenants yielding 260,000 series.
cap: Metric labels multiply series combinatorially, making high-cardinality identifiers like request ID suitable only for traces and logs.

name: p4-2026-hypothesis-matrix
title: Ranking Hypotheses by Likelihood and Test Cost
anchor: ### 3. Narrate hypotheses in order of likelihood and cost to test
spec: Two-part diagram. Left: a 2x2 prioritization matrix with X-axis 'Cost to Test' (Low to High) and Y-axis 'Likelihood' (Low to High). Top-Left quadrant (High Likelihood, Low Cost): labeled 'Test 1st (Horses)' containing 'Recent deploy or config change', tested via 1 command (rollout status, values diff) and timestamp check. Bottom-Left quadrant (Low Likelihood, Low Cost): labeled 'Test 2nd (Cheap Check)' containing 'Single bad pod', tested via per-replica metric comparison. Top-Right quadrant (High Likelihood, High Cost): labeled 'Test 3rd' containing 'Deep resource saturation / cross-zone network degradation', tested via multi-graph correlation. Bottom-Right quadrant (Low Likelihood, High Cost): labeled 'Avoid Until Last (Zebras)' containing 'Kernel bug / driver race condition', requiring kernel tracing. Right: Scientific falsification sequence in five connected blocks: 1. Observation ('p99 TTFT alert at 14:05'); 2. Hypothesis ('13:50 deploy broke cache routing'); 3. Concrete Prediction ('If true: prefix cache hit ratio dropped at 13:52 across all replicas; If false: hit ratio flat'); 4. Decisive Test ('Query vllm:prefix_cache_hits / queries'); 5. Verdict ('Ratio fell from 0.55 to 0.03 -> Confirmed, roll back; If unchanged -> Hypothesis killed, proceed to next rank').
alt: A 2x2 matrix ranking incident hypotheses by likelihood versus cost to test alongside a five-step scientific falsification loop.
cap: Rank hypotheses by likelihood and cost to test, and formulate predictions that can decisively kill a theory before investigating zebras.

name: p4-2026-drill-scorecard
title: Drill Runner Architecture and 100-Point Scorecard
spec: Layout in two vertical tiers. Top tier: Session Event Loop. User input box on the left shows slash commands (/sev, /roles, /hyp, /do, /status, /cause, /hint, /done) and plain text questions ('Can I see the golden-signals dashboard?'). Arrow labeled 'session.log(kind, text)' feeds into Session State box (tracking monotonic elapsed time, 30-minute countdown, revealed question keys, hint counter). Bottom tier: 100-Point Scorecard Evaluation Pipeline. Event stream splits into seven parallel scoring evaluators matching the chapter code: 1. 'Take Control (15 pts)': sev declared <= 120s (5), roles declared <= 120s (5), impact/dashboard asked before first action (5); 2. 'Evidence Gathered (25 pts)': proportion of must_ask keys revealed; 3. 'Hypotheses (15 pts)': >=2 hypotheses (5), first is cheap/likely (5), names root cause (5); 4. 'Mitigation (20 pts)': points awarded for required mitigation actions (up to 20); 5. 'Order (5 pts)': mitigation /do strictly before root cause /cause; 6. 'Status Cadence (10 pts)': 1 update per 10 minutes elapsed; 7. 'Safety (10 pts)': starts at 10, -5 per destructive trap (e.g. restart all pods, defrag live etcd). Right side shows Hint Penalty (-2 pts per hint) and Final Grade Thresholds: >=85 'strong', >=70 'pass', <70 'repeat this drill'.
alt: Architecture of the interview drill runner showing slash commands feeding an event log evaluated across seven scorecard categories totalling 100 points.
cap: The drill runner evaluates session timing and actions across seven rubric categories, rewarding prompt control, structured evidence gathering, and safe mitigation order.

name: p4-2028-dossier-linter-pipeline
title: Architecture and Rule Passes of the Dossier Checker
spec: Flowchart diagram oriented left-to-right showing how c28_dossier_check.py processes a project dossier. Left box: 'Input: dossier.md'. Arrow to Stage 1 'strip_comments()': replaces HTML comments with newline preserving exact line counts. Arrow to Stage 2 'Parser: Heading & Block AST': splits lines on '##' (SECTIONS: Context, My role, Constraints, Numbers, Architecture, Decisions, Failures, Changes, Metrics), '###' (blocks), and bullets ('- Label: Value'). Arrow to Stage 3 'Rules Engine (6 checks)': Box with 6 distinct audit rules: 1) 'Missing/Empty Sections' (checks 9 required sections), 2) 'Placeholder Scanner' (regex matches [YOUR...], TODO, TBD), 3) 'Numeric Line Count' (Numbers >= 3, Metrics >= 2, Failures >= 1), 4) 'Decision Block Audit' (>= 3 decisions, >= 2 alternatives per decision), 5) 'Field Completeness' (checks chosen, alternatives, why, cost accepted), 6) 'Unquantified Claim Regex' (flags 'faster', 'slower', 'massive', 'greatly' if line lacks digits). Stage 3 branches to two outputs: Bottom output 'Findings list & line numbers' -> 'exit code 1'; Top output 'summary: clean' -> 'exit code 0'. Annotate that it checks structure and completeness, not factual truth.
alt: Flowchart showing the dossier checker parsing markdown into sections and blocks, evaluating six rule sets including placeholders, numbers, and unquantified claims, and yielding an exit code.
cap: Figure 20.28.13. Parsing and validation pipeline of c28_dossier_check.py, illustrating how structural completeness, numeric density, and unquantified claims are audited.
